For
s=0,\,1/2
, these equations with
M=0
are Weyl invariant
63
63

63

A Weyl transformation is a local rescaling of the metric
g_{\mu\nu}\mapsto\Omega^{2}(x)g_{\mu\nu}

[
84
]
.

(if
\phi
and
\chi
given proper Weyl weights)
and they can be generalised Weyl-invariantly to arbitrary dimension
[
85
]
.
64
64

64

Without transforming
m
,
equation

3.18a
with
M=0
should be written as
\Delta_{0}\phi+R/6\,\phi=0
to be Weyl invariant.

As explained in
[
84
]
, Weyl invariance together with diffeomorphism invariance implies conformal invariance (although conformal invariance and diffeomorphism invariance do not imply Weyl invariance
[
84
,
86
]
as sometimes claimed
[
87
]
).
One can show that
equations

3.18a
and
3.18b
with
M=0
imply that
\phi
and
\chi
propagate on the local light cones in AdS by using that
\mathrm{d}s^{2}=0
is Weyl invariant and that
\mathrm{AdS}_{4}
is related, locally, to four-dimensional Minkowski spacetime via a Weyl transformation
[
85
]
.

While for
s<1
, we may define masslessness by requiring propagation on the local light cones, the situation for
s\geq 1
is different.
Here, we instead define masslessness by requiring gauge invariance.
In
d=4
Minkowski space,
p^{2}=0
implies, via the group theory of the Poincaré group, that the particle only has two states (helicity), see
section

2.1.2
.
However, to reduce the number of propagating degrees of freedom to two for
s\geq 1
, gauge invariance is needed, whence propagation on the light cone and gauge invariance coincide
[
85
]
.
This is not the case in arbitrary spacetimes.
Maxwell theory, that is,
s=1
, is Weyl invariant in precisely
d=4
and photons, therefore, propagate on the local light cones in
\mathrm{AdS}_{4}
, by the above argument
[
85
]
.
The gauge-invariant
s=3/2,\,2
theories are, however, not Weyl invariant in
d=4
and the fields propagate not only on but also in the interior of the light cone
[
85
]
.

Another peculiarity regarding masses in AdS is the bound for perturbative stability.
For
s>0
, the requirement is
M^{2}\geq 0
, just as in Minkowski spacetime
[
19
]
.
Remarkably, for
s=0
, only
M^{2}\geq-m^{2}
is required to avoid exponentially growing modes for small field fluctuations
[
12
,
13
]
.
This is known as the Breitenlohner–Freedman bound.
A theory in which all scalar fields satisfy the Breitenlohner–Freedman bound and all
s>0
fields satisfy
M^{2}\geq 0
is said to be BF stable.
BF stability does not imply perturbative stability since the slope of the potential can be nonvanishing, as signalled by a tadpole.

3.2.2
Masses from operators on the internal space

As stated above, the masses of the fields in
\mathrm{AdS}_{4}
are related to differential operators on the internal space.
We will not give a derivation of the mass operators for the Freund–Rubin ansatz but make some comments on the derivation.
For details, see
[
19
]
.
To derive the mass operators, one writes the
D=11
fields as their background values plus a fluctuation (for instance,
g_{MN}(x,y)=\mathring{g}_{MN}(x,y)+h_{MN}(x,y)
for the metric) and derives the linearised field equations from
D=11
supergravity using the background values of the Freund–Rubin ansatz.
Then, gauge conditions are imposed and the fluctuations are expanded in modes on the internal space, similar to what we did when discussing supersymmetry in
section

3.1
.
Finally, the mass operators are derived by analysing the equations resulting from inserting the expansions in the linearised field equations and comparing with
equation

3.18
.
The result is presented in
table

3.1
.

To make the below results plausible, note that, for instance,
h_{\mu\nu}
is a scalar on the internal space and will, hence, be expanded in scalar modes.
Since
s=2
corresponds to the transverse and traceless part of
h_{\mu\nu}
, the
s=2
mass operator must act on scalar fields on
\mathcal{M}_{7}
.

The operators appearing in
table

3.1
are the Hodge–de Rham operator
\Delta_{p}
acting on transverse
p
-forms with
p=0,\,1,\,2
; the Lichnerowicz operator
\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}
acting on transverse traceless symmetric rank-2 tensors; the Dirac operator
\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}
acting on Majorana spinors and transverse
\Gamma
-traceless Majorana vector-spinors and the operator
Q
acting on transverse 3-forms (defined in
equation

3.35
).
65
65

65

Transversality means that
\nabla^{m}Y_{mn}=0
et cetera and a vector-spinor is
\Gamma
-traceless if
\Gamma^{m}\psi_{m}=0
.

At this point, we switch to consider fields with flat indices on the internal space.
In particular,
\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}_{3/2}
acts both on the vector and spinor index of the vector-spinor.
All operators should be interpreted in terms of their eigenvalues.
Note that all of the operators are self-adjoint and respect the transversality and tracelessness conditions, whence there are bases of eigenmodes with real eigenvalues spanning the corresponding function spaces.
We discuss this further in
section

3.2.4
.

In the derivation of
table

3.1
, some special cases arise.
In the table, the subscripts label various towers of fields with the first (second) subscript referring to the top (bottom) sign or, for
\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}
and
Q
, the positive (negative) part of the spectrum of the operator.

Singletons have no Poincaré analogue and are topological in the sense that the fields have no degrees of freedom in the bulk, only on the boundary

Still, as explained in

Note that there is precisely one massless spin-

This is reassuring.
From

As is clear from

From

Similarly, unbroken gauge symmetries correspond to

eigenvalues of
\Delta_{1}
in

(

has no zero-mode on compact Einstein spaces with positive curvature

There can be additional unbroken gauge symmetries from zero-modes of

These come from the Abelian gauge invariance in

[

68
68

68

This is true of the supergravity fields; the M2 and M5-branes of M-theory, and the corresponding supergravity solutions, are electrically and magnetically charged under this symmetry, respectively.

Note that the masses of spins
3/2
,
1/2
and
0^{-}
are sensitive to skew-whiffing,

.
Also, by the skew-whiffing theorem, there are no spin-

.
By the same argument, a vacuum with
\mathcal{N}=0
related to a supersymmetric vacuum by skew-whiffing has exactly as many spin-
1/2
singletons as there are supersymmetries in the other vacuum.
As we will see below, the only supermultiplet containing singletons is the Dirac singleton supermultiplet.
Thus, there are no spin-
0
singletons in supersymmetric vacua, except for the round
S^{7}
, nor their skew-whiffed partners since the
0^{+}
spectrum is insensitive to skew-whiffing.
In fact, one can prove that the first nonzero eigenvalue of

is at least

with equality only for the round

[

]
, whence there are never spin-

From

3.1
, one can also draw some conclusions regarding BF stability.
Firstly, there cannot be any negative

values in

,
3/2_{1,2}
,

,

One can prove that

Since

The only remaining tower is

This criterion is not satisfied by all compact Einstein spaces with positive curvature

]

If the vacuum is supersymmetric, it is perturbatively stable (see below)

]
.
Since the

As remarked above, this does not imply that they are perturbatively stable.

One class of unstable solutions are Riemannian products.
If
\mathcal{M}_{7}=\mathcal{M}_{(1)}\times\mathcal{M}_{(2)}
with the product metric, that is,
g_{mn}
is block diagonal over the two factors, then there is a mode of
\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}
with eigenvalue
0<3m^{2}
corresponding to one of the factors expanding while the other contracts
[
14
]
.

3.2.3
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,2)
-representations and supersymmetry

Similar to what we described in
section

2.1.2
, elementary particles in
\mathrm{AdS}_{4}
correspond to nontrivial irreducible unitary representations of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,2)
, the double cover of the identity component of the isometry group
{\mathrm{SO}}(3,2)
of
\mathrm{AdS}_{4}
.
We denote the generators of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,2)
by
M_{\hat{\alpha}\hat{\beta}}
where
\hat{\alpha},\hat{\beta},\ldots
are 5-dimensional indices.

\mathrm{AdS}_{4}
is the universal cover of the connected hyperboloid
\smash{\eta_{\hat{\alpha}\hat{\beta}}x^{\hat{\alpha}}x^{\hat{\beta}}=-1/(2m)^{2}}

[
89
]
.
69
69

69

For example in
[
90
]
, AdS is used for the hyperboloid and CAdS for the cover.

We split the 5-dimensional index as
\hat{\alpha}=(\alpha,5)
in the basis in which
\eta_{\hat{\alpha}\hat{\beta}}
is block-diagonal with blocks
\eta_{\alpha\beta}
and
-1
.
By considering the Poincaré limit

, one sees that

and

are the AdS analogues of the Lorentz and momentum generators of the Poincaré algebra, respectively
[

]

Hence,
M_{05}
is identified as a dimensionless energy operator.
We consider representations with energy bounded from below, that is, for which there is a smallest eigenvalue
E_{0}
of
M_{05}
.
The algebra
{\mathfrak{so}}(3,2)
is of rank 2 and irreducible representations can, hence, be specified by the eigenvalues of two Casimir operators
[
91
]
.
Equivalently, and more physically relevant, the irreducible representations can be denoted by
D(E_{0},s)
where
E_{0}
is the lowest energy eigenvalue in the representation and
s
the spin
70
70

70

The spin is, as usual, defined via the Casimir of the
{\mathfrak{so}}(3)
corresponding to spatial rotations.

of the particle
[
89
]
.
A representation is said to be unitary if there exists an invariant, positive definite scalar product on it.
One can start from
2s+1
lowest energy states and construct an invariant scalar product by declaring that these are orthonormal and that the generators are (anti-)Hermitian (depending on conventions).
Demanding that the scalar product is positive definite then leads to unitarity bounds on
E_{0}

[
89
]
.
71
71

71

Actually, it is sufficient to demand positive semi-definiteness and then factor out the zero norm states. This leads to multiplet shortening and corresponds to saturating the inequalities in
equation

3.21
. See
[
89
]
for details.

The result of this analysis is that

s<1\colon\quad E_{0}\geq s+\frac{1}{2},\qquad\qquad s\geq 1\colon\quad E_{0}\geq s+1.

(3.21)

There are some special representations.
These are the massless
D(2,0)
and, for all
s
,
D(s+1,s)
and the Dirac singleton representations

and
D(1,1/2)

[

]

The lowest energy eigenvalue,
E_{0}
, characterising a representation can be related to the AdS mass

discussed above.
Here, we do not give a derivation but simply quote the result in

[

]
.
The sign ambiguities for

arise from a quadratic equation and are eliminated for

by the unitarity bounds.
72
72

[

For unitarity and

is required for the plus sign, again the Breitenlohner–Freedman bound, and
-m^{2}\leq M^{2}_{s=0}\leq 3m^{2}
for the minus sign.
For the spinors, all real

are allowed for the plus sign and
|M_{s=1/2}|\leq m
for the minus sign.
One can prove that the absolute values of the eigenvalues of

are greater than or equal to

[

Lastly, for

3.2.4
Differential operators and a universal Laplacian

Here, we discuss some properties of the operators appearing in
table

3.1
and relate them to a universal Laplacian.
We assume that the compact manifold
\mathcal{M}_{7}
is without boundary or that the boundary conditions are such that all boundary integrals vanish.
To see where the universal Laplacian comes from, consider first the Hodge–de Rham operator, or Hodge Laplacian,

\Delta_{p}=\delta\mathrm{d}+\mathrm{d}\delta,

(3.24)

acting on
p
-forms.
Here,
\mathrm{d}
is the exterior derivative and
\delta
the codifferential, see
appendix

D
.
A
p
-form
\alpha
is transverse if
\delta\alpha=0
, which follows from the definition
\mathcal{D}^{b}a_{ba_{1}\ldots a_{p-1}}=0
of transversality and the component formula for
\delta\alpha
.
Thus,
\Delta_{p}
maps transverse
p
-forms to transverse
p
-forms since
\delta\Delta_{p}\alpha=\delta\mathrm{d}\delta\alpha
.
Also,
\Delta_{p}
is manifestly self-adjoint and nonnegative since
\delta
is the adjoint of
\mathrm{d}
.

By using the definitions of the exterior derivative
\mathrm{d}
and the codifferential
\delta
we immediately find

\Delta_{p}\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}=-\square\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}-p[\mathcal{D}_{[a_{1}},\mathcal{D}^{b}]\alpha_{|b|a_{2}\ldots a_{p}]},

(3.25)

where
\mathcal{D}
is the torsion-free spin connection.
Using the Ricci identity
[\mathcal{D}_{a},\mathcal{D}_{b}]=R_{abcd}\Sigma^{cd}
, this can be written as

\displaystyle\Delta_{p}\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}

\displaystyle=-\square\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}-[\mathcal{D}_{b_{1}},\mathcal{D}_{b_{2}}]\Sigma^{b_{1}b_{2}}\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}=

\displaystyle=-\square\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}-R_{b_{1}b_{2}c_{1}c_{2}}\Sigma^{c_{1}c_{2}}\Sigma^{b_{1}b_{2}}\alpha_{a_{1}\ldots a_{p}}.

Thus, we define

\Delta\coloneqq-\square-[\mathcal{D}_{a_{1}},\mathcal{D}_{a_{2}}]\Sigma^{a_{1}a_{2}}=-\square-R_{a_{1}a_{2}b_{1}b_{2}}\Sigma^{a_{1}a_{2}}\Sigma^{b_{1}b_{2}}.

(3.29)

We refer to this as the
universal Laplacian
since it can act on a field carrying any representation of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(7)
and, as we will see, is related to all the other Laplacians we are interested in.

Let us show that
\Delta
is self-adjoint.
To this end, let
Y_{A}
be a field carrying any finite-dimensional real representation of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(7)
.
75
75

75

We restrict to the real case since that is what we are interested in and for notational convenience. What follows is easily generalised to the complex case by replacing the symmetric invariant
\delta^{AB}
with a Hermitian invariant
\delta^{\bar{A}B}
.

Since
{\mathrm{Spin}}(7)
is compact, the representation is unitary and there is an invariant symmetric nondegenerate
\delta^{AB}
with Euclidean signature.
We have an
L^{2}
inner product defined by

\langle Y,X\rangle=\int\mathrm{vol}\,Y_{A}\delta^{AB}X_{B}.

(3.30)

To see that
\Delta
is self-adjoint with respect to this inner product, note that

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \langle Y,-\square X\rangle&=-\int\mathrm{vol}\,Y_{A}\delta^{AB}\square X_{B}=+\int\mathrm{vol}\,\mathcal{D}_{a}Y_{A}\delta^{ab}\delta^{AB}\mathcal{D}_{b}X_{B}=\\
&=-\int\mathrm{vol}\,\square Y_{A}\delta^{AB}X_{B}=\langle-\square Y,X\rangle,\end{aligned}

(3.31a)

\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \langle Y,-\mathcal{D}_{a}\mathcal{D}_{b}\Sigma^{ab}X\rangle&=-\int\mathrm{vol}\,Y_{A}(\Sigma^{ab})^{AB}\mathcal{D}_{a}\mathcal{D}_{b}X_{B}=\\
&=+\int\mathrm{vol}\,\mathcal{D}_{a}Y_{A}(\Sigma^{ab})^{AB}\mathcal{D}_{b}X_{B}=\\
&=-\int\mathrm{vol}\,\mathcal{D}_{b}\mathcal{D}_{a}Y_{A}(\Sigma^{ab})^{AB}X_{B}=\langle-\mathcal{D}_{a}\mathcal{D}_{b}\Sigma^{ab}Y,X\rangle,\end{aligned}

(3.31b)

where we have used
\delta^{AB}
to raise an index on
(\Sigma^{ab})_{A}{}^{B}
, that
\delta^{AB}
and
(\Sigma^{ab})^{AB}
are invariant tensors and, in the last step, that
(\Sigma^{ab})^{AB}
is antisymmetric both in
a\,b
and
A\,B
.
The last statement follows from
\delta^{AB}
being a symmetric invariant.
Thus, glossing over some mathematical subtleties regarding the distinction between symmetric and self-adjoint unbounded operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces
[
95
]
,
\Delta
is self-adjoint and there is a basis of eigenmodes of
\Delta
with real eigenvalues.

We would also like to show that
\Delta
respects the various conditions (transversality, tracelessness, et cetera) placed on the fields.
We do this separately in the cases of interest.
Since
\Delta=\Delta_{p}
when acting on
p
-forms and
\Delta_{p}
respects transversality,
\Delta
can be restricted to transverse
p
-forms.

(3.34)

Since the right-hand sides of
equations

3.33
and
3.34
cancel when combined as in
equation

3.32
,
\Delta_{\mathrm{L}}
can indeed be restricted to the space of transverse
h_{ab}
.

Next, we turn to the 3-form operator
Q
, defined as

Q\coloneqq\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d},

(3.35)

which maps 3-forms into 3-forms.
If
\alpha
is a transverse 3-form,

\Delta_{3}\alpha=\delta\mathrm{d}\alpha=\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}\alpha=Q^{2}\alpha,

(3.36)

since
\delta
is acting on the 4-form
\mathrm{d}\alpha
.
This gives the relation between
Q
and the Laplacian
\Delta
.
In seven dimensions and Euclidean signature,
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}^{2}=1
,
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}
is self-adjoint and, thus,

Q^{\ast}=\delta\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}=\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}^{2}=Q,

(3.37)

that is,
Q
is self-adjoint.
Also,
Q
maps into transverse 3-forms since
\delta Q=-\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}^{2}=0
.

Turning now to half-integer spins, the relevant operator is the Dirac operator

\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}=\mathrm{i}\Gamma^{a}\mathcal{D}_{a}.

(3.38)

The Dirac operator
\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}
maps Majorana spinors to Majorana spinors.
This is easily seen in the basis from
section

C.1
since the Majorana condition then reduces to a reality condition for each component and
\Gamma_{a}
are purely imaginary.
It also maps the space of transverse
\Gamma
-traceless vector-spinors, that is, vector-spinors
\psi_{a}
satisfying
\mathcal{D}^{a}\psi_{a}=0=\Gamma^{a}\psi_{a}
, to itself since

\displaystyle\Gamma^{a}\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}\psi_{a}=-\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}\Gamma^{a}\psi_{a}+2\mathrm{i}\mathcal{D}^{a}\psi_{a}=0,

The Dirac operator can also be considered in the context of Dirac spinors. In this case, one should use the Dirac conjugate instead of the Majorana conjugate in the
L^{2}
inner product. The eigenvalues are the same since the Majorana eigenbasis provides an eigenbasis for the space of Dirac spinors as well.

\displaystyle\langle\psi,\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}\chi\rangle

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{vol}\,\psi_{A}^{\mathrm{T}}C\delta^{AB}\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}\chi_{B}=\int\mathrm{vol}\,\mathrm{i}\mathcal{D}^{a}\psi_{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\Gamma_{a}^{\mathrm{T}}C\delta^{AB}\chi_{B}=

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{vol}\,(\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}\psi_{A})^{\mathrm{T}}C\delta^{AB}\chi_{B}=\langle\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}\psi,\chi\rangle.

(3.40)

Here, the sign from the integration by parts cancels the sign from
C\Gamma_{a}=-\Gamma_{a}^{\mathrm{T}}C
.

(3.43)

Thus, for spinors and vector-spinors, respectively,

\displaystyle(\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}})^{2}\psi=\Delta\psi+\frac{21}{4}m^{2}\psi,

(3.44a)

\displaystyle(\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}})^{2}\psi_{a}=\Delta\psi_{a}-\frac{3}{4}m^{2}\psi_{a},

(3.44b)

where we have used that
R_{ab}=6m^{2}\delta_{ab}
.
Note that, for Einstein spaces, the eigenvalues of

This seems to break down for higher tensor-spinors since the difference between

To conclude, we have seen that all of the operators

Moreover, we have found that all of the operators are related to a universal Laplacian
\Delta

equation

3.29

\Delta=-\square-R_{a_{1}a_{2}b_{1}b_{2}}\Sigma^{a_{1}a_{2}}\Sigma^{b_{1}b_{2}},

(3.45)

which differs from

4.   Homogeneous spaces

Homogeneous pseudo-Riemannian
77
77

77

We include all signatures of the metric in “pseudo-Riemannian”.

manifolds are a rich, yet particularly simple, set of manifolds.
Due to this, they are often used as the internal space in string and supergravity compactifications.
Examples of homogeneous spaces include Euclidean spaces, spheres, flat tori and hyperbolic spaces in Euclidean signature; Minkowski, de Sitter (dS) and anti-de Sitter (AdS) spaces in Lorentzian signature and super-Minkowski and super-AdS superspaces.

A homogeneous space is, intuitively, a space in which all points are equivalent, or “look the same”, in some sense appropriate to the setting.
Technically, it is a space
\mathcal{M}
on which a group
G
of automorphisms acts transitively and effectively, that is, for every
x,y\in\mathcal{M}
there is a
g\in G
such that
gx=y
and there is no
g\in G
which acts trivially on
\mathcal{M}
.
That
G
acts by automorphisms means that it preserves the structure of
\mathcal{M}
and we require
G
to act effectively since, otherwise, it is really
G/N
, where
N
is the kernel of the
G
-action, that acts on
\mathcal{M}
.
78
78

78

When considering spinor fields, we will have reason to loosen the latter requirement slightly.

Since we are interested in connected oriented pseudo-Riemannian manifolds,
the automorphisms are orientation-preserving isometries of
\mathcal{M}
, that is,
G\subseteq\operatorname{Iso}_{+}(\mathcal{M})
.
So, a homogeneous (pseudo-Riemannian) manifold is a manifold on which the isometry group acts transitively.
The isometry group is a Lie group
[
96
,
97
]
, whence, in the following, we consider Lie groups
G
.

The stabiliser
H_{y}
of
y\in\mathcal{M}
, that is, the subgroup of
G
fixing
y
, is called the isotropy group of
y
.
It is easy to see that the isotropy groups of different points in
\mathcal{M}
are conjugate subgroups in
G
.
Thus, we often need not distinguish between them and simply write
H
for
the
isotropy subgroup, which is a closed subgroup of
G

[
80
]
.
79
79

79

A closed subgroup of a Lie group is a Lie subgroup by Cartan’s theorem.

Note that the isotropy group
H_{y}
is a subgroup of
{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(T_{y}\mathcal{M})
, where
g
is the
G
-invariant metric on
\mathcal{M}
.
80
80

80

With
{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(V)
we mean the orientation-preserving subgroup of
{\mathrm{GL}}(V)
that leaves the metric
g
on
V
invariant.

This follows from the fact that an isometry of a connected manifold is determined by its value and differential at a single point
[
80
]
.
Thus, since an element of
H_{y}
fixes
y
, it is completely determined by its differential at
y
.
Since
H_{y}
preserves the metric and orientation on
\mathcal{M}
, and particularly on the tangent space at the fixed point,
T_{y}\mathcal{M}
, there is a natural homomorphism
H_{y}\to{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(T_{y}\mathcal{M})
and we may view
H_{y}
as a subgroup of
{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(T_{y}\mathcal{M})
.

G
is a principal
H
-bundle over
\mathcal{M}

[
98
]
.
For an introduction to fibre bundles, see
section

E.1
.
Similar to the frame bundle, we may view
G
as the bundle of
H
-frames over
\mathcal{M}
.
To see this, pick an orthonormal frame at a point
o
and use the pushforward by every element in
g
to get a set of frames.
This set is naturally in one-to-one correspondence with
G
since
G
acts effectively and isometries are determined by their value and differential at a single point.
Due to
G
preserving the metric of
\mathcal{M}
, the set will only contain orthonormal frames.
Thus,
G
is a subbundle of the orthonormal frame bundle and we have a reduction of the structure group from
{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(\dim\mathcal{M})
to
H
.

By choosing an origin
o\in\mathcal{M}
we get a natural map
\phi\colon G/H_{o}\to\mathcal{M}
by
\phi(gH_{o})=go
.
It is easy to see that
\phi
is a well-defined bijection and it is, in fact, a diffeomorphism
[
80
]
.
The
G
-action on
\mathcal{M}
is realised on
G/H
by left-multiplication.
By pulling back the
G
-invariant metric on
\mathcal{M}
to
G/H
, the two spaces become isometric whence we do not distinguish them in the following.

Instead of starting from a manifold
\mathcal{M}
and then realising it as a coset space (provided that the isometry group acts transitively), one can start from the groups
G
and
H
and construct a homogeneous manifold as
G/H
.
We do this in
section

4.1
.
Note, however, that there might exist a proper subgroup of
\operatorname{Iso}_{+}(\mathcal{M})
which acts transitively on
\mathcal{M}

[
99
]
, in which case
\mathcal{M}
can be described by different cosets
G/H
.
Also, if we loosen the requirement that
G
acts effectively, it may be possible to describe
\mathcal{M}
by additional cosets
[
19
]
.
In
section

4.2
, we discuss harmonic analysis on coset spaces.

4.1
Geometry

Let
G
be a Lie group and
H
a closed subgroup with Lie algebras
\mathfrak{g}
and
\mathfrak{h}
, respectively.
We will assume that the algebras are reductive, that is, that there exists an
\operatorname{Ad}(H)
-invariant subspace
\mathfrak{m}
of
\mathfrak{g}
such that
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{m}

[
80
]
.
Here,
\operatorname{Ad}
is the adjoint representation of
G
.
Thus, reductivity means that the adjoint representation of
G
splits, when restricted to
H
, into a direct sum of the adjoint representation of
H
and another representation.
The latter is a
H
-representation on
\mathfrak{m}\simeq T_{o}\mathcal{M}
called the isotropy representation
[
99
]
.
This implies that
[\mathfrak{h},\mathfrak{m}]\subseteq\mathfrak{m}
while the converse implication holds for connected
H

[
99
]
.
Reductivity is not a very restrictive assumption: every homogeneous space admitting a
G
-invariant metric with Euclidean signature is reductive
[
99
]
.
Since we are, in this thesis, interested in compact manifolds with Euclidean signature to be used in a Kaluza–Klein compactification, we find this assumption acceptable.

In the above, we assumed that the
G
-action on
\mathcal{M}
is effective.
When constructing a coset space, it is natural to ask what this means for
G
and
H
.
Since any element
g\in G
which acts trivially on
\mathcal{M}
in particular fixes
o
, it follows that
g\in H_{o}
.
Since an element of
H_{o}
is determined by its differential at
o
, that is, its action on
T_{o}\mathcal{M}
, this implies that the
G
-action is effective if and only if the isotropy representation of
H
is faithful.

We wish to put a
G
-invariant metric on
G/H
.
By a theorem
[
80
]
,
G
-invariant tensor fields on
G/H
are in one-to-one correspondence with
H
-invariant tensors of the same type on
\mathfrak{m}
.
Thus, for a
G
-invariant metric on
G/H
we need a
H
-invariant symmetric nondegenerate rank-2 tensor.
Note that, if there is only one such tensor (up to a constant factor), the coset space
G/H
, equipped with the
G
-invariant metric, is an Einstein space, since the Ricci-tensor will also be proportional to the invariant
[
19
]
.
This happens if the isotropy representation is irreducible
[
100
]
.

.

(4.9)

Since
\omega_{abc}
is antisymmetric in its last two indices
\omega_{abc}=\omega_{[ab]c}-\omega_{[ac]b}-\omega_{[bc]a}
, where we have lowered the last index using
g_{ab}
, whence

\omega_{abc}=-\frac{1}{2}F_{abc}-\Omega_{a}^{i}f_{ibc},\qquad F_{abc}\coloneqq 2f_{a[bc]}-f_{bca}.

(4.14)

Lastly, we mention that there is a special class of
G
-invariant metrics which are particularly simple.
Consider a positive definite
G
-invariant tensor
g_{AB}
.
One can then take
\mathfrak{m}
as the orthogonal complement of
\mathfrak{h}
.
This makes
g_{AB}
block-diagonal on
\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{m}
and
g_{ab}
, the restriction to
\mathfrak{m}
,
H
-invariant.
Such a metric
g_{ab}
is said to be a normal homogeneous metric on
G/H

[
99
]
.
Since
g_{AB}
is
G
-invariant and block-diagonal,
f_{abc}
is completely antisymmetric and
F_{abc}=f_{abc}
.
Then,
equation

simplifies to

Spin geometry

To be able to globally define spinors on
\mathcal{M}=G/H
, it must admit a spin structure, that is, a lift of the structure group from
{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
to
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
.
84
84

84

For a proper introduction to spin structures and spin geometry, see
[
73
]
.

Not all coset spaces
G/H
admit a spin structure, for instance
\mathbb{C}\mathbf{P}^{2}\simeq{\mathrm{SU}}(3)/{\mathrm{U}}(2)
does not
[
98
]
.
Therefore, like
[
98
]
, we assume that there is a covering group
\bar{G}
of
G
such that the embedding of
H
in
{\mathrm{SO}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
lifts
to an embedding of the corresponding cover
\bar{H}
of
H
in
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
.
This implies that
\mathcal{M}\simeq\bar{G}/\bar{H}
where
\bar{H}
is a subgroup of
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
.
The
\bar{G}
-action on
\mathcal{M}
is not effective since the lift is nontrivial.
However, it is infinitesimally effective in the sense that the isotropy representation of
\bar{\mathfrak{h}}=\mathfrak{h}
is faithful.

Analogous to what we saw above,
\bar{G}
is a principal
\bar{H}
-bundle over
\mathcal{M}
and we have a reduction of the structure group from
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
to
\bar{H}

[
98
]
.
Correspondingly, the associated vector bundles of the principal bundle of spin frames split into direct sums of vector bundles carrying irreducible
\bar{H}
-representations.
This means that tensor and spinor fields on
\mathcal{M}
can be decomposed (globally) into pieces transforming under some representation of
\bar{H}
.

4.2
Harmonic analysis

In this section, we discuss harmonic analysis on coset spaces, a generalisation of Fourier series and spherical harmonics.
Harmonic analysis on coset spaces is important in Kaluza–Klein compactifications since, if the
(4+k)
-dimensional theory is compactified on a manifold which is locally isometric to
\mathcal{M}_{4}\times\mathcal{M}_{k}
, the fields can be expanded on
\mathcal{M}_{k}
using harmonics with spacetime fields as coefficients, yielding a
4
-dimensional theory, see for instance
[
19
,
98
]
.

We assume that the manifold is spin and that the group of effective isometries lifts as described in
section

4.1
.
Since we will only be concerned with the lifted groups, we denote the lifted isometry group by
G
and the lifted isotropy group, which is a subgroup of
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathfrak{m})
, by
H
.
Also, since the isometry group of a compact manifold is compact
[
101
]
and the representation theory of compact Lie groups is particularly well behaved, we restrict our attention to compact
G
.
The relevant theory is based on the Peter–Weyl theorem and the fact that
G
is a principal
H
-bundle over
G/H
.

\delta_{\bar{P}Q}

[
102
]

Coset harmonics

Consider now a tensor (or spinor) field on a coset space
G/H
, that is, a section of a vector bundle over
\mathcal{M}
carrying a particular representation of

As explained above, these bundles split into direct sums of vector bundles carrying irreducible
H
-representations due to the reduction of the structure group from

to the subgroup
H

Thus, we wish to find a basis for vector bundles with

Such bundles are constructed from a vector space

Lastly, we expand on the link between sections of

A well-known example is the expansion of a scalar field on

4.3
The coset master equation

In this section, we discuss what we will refer to as
the coset master equation
, which we will use to compute the eigenvalue spectrum of the squashed
S^{7}
in
chapter

6
.
The equation is based on the fact that the tensor and spinor fields can be expanded in terms of harmonics that come from the irreducible representations of
G
, as described in the preceding section.
For reasons explained below, we restrict our attention to normal homogeneous metrics, so that
F_{abc}=f_{abc}
is completely antisymmetric, and compact Euclidean manifolds
\mathcal{M}
.

As explained above,
G
is a principal
H
-bundle over
\mathcal{M}
.
There is a natural principal
H
-connection on this bundle induced by the splitting
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{m}

[

]

In our local coordinates, the

[
20
]

\check{\mathcal{D}}_{m}=\partial_{m}+\Omega_{m}^{i}T_{i}.

(4.26)

Let

Then, by

\check{\mathcal{D}}_{a}\rho(L_{y}^{-1})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.16771pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.16771pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.82642pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.73315pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{(Q)}}}_{{{P}\mathchoice{\makebox[12.5478pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[12.5478pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[7.68481pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.48917pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=-(T_{a})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.16771pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.16771pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.82642pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.73315pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{R}}}_{{{P}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.06009pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.06009pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.75835pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.68454pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}\rho(L_{y}^{-1})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.06009pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.06009pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.75835pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.68454pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{(Q)}}}_{{{R}\mathchoice{\makebox[12.5478pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[12.5478pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[7.68481pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.48917pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}},

where

This is what we will refer to as the coset master equation.
From

92

For semisimple

The normalisation here might not be conventional for concrete cases.

Here,

where

and
\check{\square}\coloneqq g^{ab}\check{\mathcal{D}}_{a}\check{\mathcal{D}}_{b}

We will refer to this equation as the quadratic master equation.

94

94

This has been referred to as the squared coset master equation in, for instance,
[

]
. Since only the operators are squared, we use “quadratic” instead.

As noted above, the field

splits into irreducible
H
-components each carrying an induced
G
-representation.

\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{h}}
acts by a constant on each irreducible
H
-component and can thus be implemented as a matrix acting on the spin-index of

acts by a constant on each irreducible

As we saw in
section

3.2.4
, the mass spectrum of a Freund–Rubin compactification is related to the eigenvalue spectrum of a universal Laplacian
equation

3.45

\Delta Y=\kappa^{2}Y,\qquad\quad\Delta\coloneqq-\square-R_{abcd}\Sigma^{ab}\Sigma^{cd}.

(4.32)

Since
\mathcal{M}
is compact and Euclidean, both
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathcal{M})
and
G
are compact, the finite-dimensional representations of
{\mathrm{Spin}}_{g}(\mathcal{M})
are unitary and the fields carrying such representations form a unitary
G
-representation, with respect to the appropriate
L^{2}
inner product, which is, thus, completely reducible.
Hence, the eigenmodes of
\Delta
fall into irreducible representations of
G
since
\Delta
is manifestly invariant under isometries.

To be able to use
equation

4.31
to compute the eigenvalues of
\Delta
, we wish to relate
\square
and
\check{\square}
.
Using
equation

4.28
, that

and

is an

-invariant for any representation

, we find

\displaystyle\check{\square}

\displaystyle=\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}\Bigl(\mathcal{D}_{a}+\frac{1}{2}f_{abc}\Sigma^{bc}\Bigr)=\square+\frac{1}{2}f^{ade}\Sigma_{de}\mathcal{D}_{a}+\frac{1}{2}f_{abc}\Sigma^{bc}\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}=

\displaystyle=\square+f_{abc}\Sigma^{bc}\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}-\frac{1}{4}f_{abc}f^{ade}\Sigma^{bc}\Sigma_{de}.

(4.33)

Combining this with

4.31
and
4.32
gives

f_{abc}\Sigma^{bc}\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}=\Delta-\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}+\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{h}}+R_{abcd}\Sigma^{ab}\Sigma^{cd}+\frac{1}{4}f_{abc}f^{ade}\Sigma^{bc}\Sigma_{de}.

(4.34)

We can simplify

a bit further.
For this, note that, by

(4.40)

The Ricci identity
\check{\mathcal{D}}^{2}\Omega=\check{R}\wedge\Omega
can thus be written as

[\check{\mathcal{D}}_{a},\check{\mathcal{D}}_{b}]=\check{R}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}{d}}}_{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.55038pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.8217pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}\Sigma_{cd}-\check{T}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}}}_{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}\check{\mathcal{D}}_{c}=(T^{i})_{ab}T_{i}+\mathchoice{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}}}_{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{f^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displayst (4.41)

since
\check{\mathcal{D}}^{2}\Omega=\mathcal{D}(e^{a}\mathcal{D}_{a}\Omega)=T^{a}\wedge\mathcal{D}_{a}\Omega-e^{a}\wedge e^{b}\check{\mathcal{D}}_{b}\check{\mathcal{D}}_{a}\Omega
.
Note that we raise and lower
\mathfrak{h}
-indices using
g_{ij}
.

5.   Squashed sphere geometry

In this chapter, we study the geometry of the manifold on which we will compactify eleven-dimensional supergravity: the squashed seven-sphere.
With squashing, we mean a smooth deformation of a homogeneous manifold, that is, a deformation of the metric (the topology is unchanged), that keeps the manifold homogeneous.
Although homogeneity should be preserved, the isometry group may change when squashing.
For instance, when we squash the round
S^{7}
, part of the
{\mathrm{SO}}(8)
isometry is broken.
Note that the existence of a squashing deformation is nontrivial.
For instance, one cannot squash
S^{2}

[
19
]
.

Below, we present two constructions of the squashed seven-sphere.
First, it is realised as a nontrivial principal
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
-bundle over
S^{4}
and, second, as a coset space (the subscripts are explained below)

\frac{{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{C}}{{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{A}\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{B+C}}.

(5.1)

We also discuss the relation between these constructions and an isometric embedding in the quaternionic projective space
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}
.

5.1
Squashed
S^{7}
as a principal bundle

This construction is based on the fact that
S^{7}
can be realised as a principal
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
-bundle over
S^{4}
and starts from the fact that the group of unit quaternions, which is isomorphic to
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
, has the topology of
S^{3}
.
Let
U
be a unit quaternion, parametrised by Euler angles as
[
19
]

U=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{k}\phi/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta/2}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{k}\psi/2},

(5.2)

where
\mathrm{i}
,
\mathrm{j}
and
\mathrm{k}
are the imaginary units of
\mathbb{H}
.
Consider the Lie algebra-valued 1-form

\sigma\coloneqq 2U^{-1}\mathrm{d}U=\mathrm{i}\sigma^{1}+\mathrm{j}\sigma^{2}+\mathrm{k}\sigma^{3}=h_{i}\sigma^{i},

(5.3)

which is proportional to the Maurer–Cartan form.
Here,
\sigma^{i}
are left-invariant 1-forms and
h^{i}=(\mathrm{i},\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k})^{i}
.
97
97

97

The explicit expressions for
\sigma^{i}
in terms of the Euler angles can be found in
[
19
]
.

Using
0=\mathrm{d}(U^{-1}U)=\mathrm{d}U^{-1}\>U+U^{-1}\mathrm{d}U
and
h_{i}h_{j}=-\delta_{ij}+\mathchoice{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}h_{k}
we immediately find

\mathrm{d}\sigma=-\frac{1}{2}\sigma\wedge\sigma=-\frac{1}{2}h_{i}\mathchoice{\epsilon^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}{k}}}}{\epsilon^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}{k}}}}{\epsilon^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}{k}}}}{\epsilon^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}{k}}}}\sigma^{j}\wedge\sigma^{k},

(5.4)

which is essentially the Maurer–Cartan equation.
Because of
equation

5.4
, we say that the 1-forms
\sigma^{i}
satisfy the
{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
algebra.

The quaternionic left-invariant 1-form
\sigma
and the invariant
\delta_{ij}
allows us to construct a metric on
S^{3}
as
98
98

98

Note that, by writing the metric like this, we have chosen a length unit. Thus, we work in a dimensionless unit system.

\mathrm{d}s^{2}(S^{3})=\|\sigma\|^{2}=\sigma_{i}\sigma^{i}.

(5.5)

In fact, this is the standard metric on
S^{3}
up to a constant conformal factor
[
19
]
.
That
\sigma
is left-invariant, that is, invariant under
U\mapsto aU
where
a\in{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
, is immediate from
equation

5.3
.
The metric
\|\sigma\|^{2}
is, however, right-invariant as well, that is, invariant under
U\mapsto Ua
, since then
\sigma\mapsto a^{-1}\sigma a
.
Thus, the metric is said to be bi-invariant.

From the above metric on
S^{3}
, the metric on
S^{4}
can be written as
[
19
]

\mathrm{d}s^{2}(S^{4})=\mathrm{d}\mu^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\sin^{2}{\mu}\>\|\tilde{\Sigma}\|^{2},

(5.6)

where
0<\mu<\pi
and
\tilde{\Sigma}
is a quaternionic left-invariant 1-form satisfying the
{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
algebra.
This construction uses that
S^{4}
without the north and south pole is diffeomorphic to
(0,\pi)\times S^{3}
and the
\sin^{2}\mu
factor gives the three-spheres their correct sizes, smaller close to the poles and larger closer to the ‘‘equator’’.
99
99

99

The construction is analogous to glueing together circles of various sizes along a semicircle to make a sphere.

The coordinate patch described by these coordinates is a warped product space (compare to
section

3.1
).

Now that we have briefly discussed the metrics on
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)\simeq S^{3}
and
S^{4}
we turn to the real case of interest, that is, an
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
-bundle over
S^{4}
.
We now have two
S^{3}
manifolds and use one real coordinate,
\mu
, and two unit quaternions
\tilde{U},\tilde{V}
.
Hence, there are two independent
{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
algebras and we need two sets of imaginary units,
h_{i}^{\tilde{U}}
and
h_{i}^{\tilde{V}}
.
Let
\tilde{\sigma}=h_{i}^{\tilde{U}}\tilde{\sigma}^{i}
and
\tilde{\Sigma}=h_{i}^{\tilde{V}}\tilde{\Sigma}^{i}
be the
{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
-forms, constructed as in
equation

5.3
, corresponding to the two unit quaternion coordinates.
A metric can then be written as

\mathrm{d}s^{2}=\mathrm{d}\mu^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\sin^{2}{\mu}\>\|\tilde{\Sigma}\|^{2}+\lambda^{2}\|\tilde{\sigma}-A\|^{2},

(5.7)

where
A=h_{i}^{\tilde{U}}A^{i}
is a Yang–Mills
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
gauge potential.
With
A=0
this would just be
S^{4}\times S^{3}
, with
\lambda
determining the relative size of the factors, but if the potential describes a topologically nontrivial instanton, the topology of the bundle is affected
[
19
]
.
In particular, with

A^{i}=\cos^{2}\frac{\mu}{2}\>\tilde{\Sigma}^{i},

(5.8)

the topology is that of
S^{7}

[
19
]
.
Note, however, that the topology of the chart covered by our coordinates is still that of
(0,\pi)\times S^{3}\times S^{3}
.
The parameter
\lambda
in
equation

5.7
will be referred to as the squashing parameter.

Rewriting the metric

Before computing the Riemann tensor, we rewrite the metric in
equation

5.7
as
[
19
]

\mathrm{d}s^{2}=\mathrm{d}\mu^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\sin^{2}{\mu}\>\|\varpi\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\lambda^{2}\|\nu+\cos\mu\>\varpi\|^{2},

(5.9)

where

\nu^{i}\coloneqq\sigma^{i}+\Sigma^{i},\qquad\varpi^{i}\coloneqq\sigma^{i}-\Sigma^{i},

(5.10)

where
\sigma
and
\Sigma
are quaternionic left-invariant 1-forms satisfying the
{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
algebra related to two unit quaternions
U
and
V
, respectively, as in
equation

5.3
.
This form of the metric comes from an isometric embedding of the squashed
S^{7}
in the quaternionic projective space
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}

[
19
]
.
In the isometric embedding, only
0<\lambda^{2}\leq 1
is possible
[
19
]
, although there seems to be no such upper bound on
\lambda^{2}
in
equation

5.7
.

Note that we could not have written
equation

5.10
as is without indices since
\sigma
contains
h_{i}^{U}
while
\Sigma
contains
h_{i}^{V}
.
To remedy this, we indicate which set of imaginary units is being used with a superscript as
\sigma^{U}=h_{i}^{U}\sigma^{i}
,
\sigma^{V}=h_{i}^{V}\sigma^{i}
,
\varpi^{V}=\sigma^{V}-\Sigma^{V}
and so on.
Since
\|\sigma\|=\sigma_{i}\sigma^{i}
regardless of which set of unit quaternions is being used, we need not worry about this in the metrics
equations

5.7
and
5.9
.
The relation between the two constructions is

\tilde{\sigma}^{V}=-V\Sigma^{V}V^{-1},\qquad\tilde{\Sigma}^{V}=V\varpi^{V}V^{-1}.

(5.11)

To see this, first note that the first and middle terms of the metrics
equations

5.7
and
5.9
are equal since
V
is a unit quaternion.
That the last terms are also equal follows from

\displaystyle\bigl\|\tilde{\sigma}-\cos^{2}\frac{\mu}{2}\,\tilde{\Sigma}\bigr\|^{2}

\displaystyle=\bigl\|\Sigma+\cos^{2}\frac{\mu}{2}\,\varpi\bigr\|^{2}=\bigl\|\Sigma+\frac{1}{2}(\sigma-\Sigma)+\frac{1}{2}\cos\mu\>\varpi\bigr\|^{2}=

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\|\nu+\cos\mu\>\varpi\|^{2}.

(5.12)

Furthermore, that
\tilde{\sigma}
from
equation

5.11
satisfies the
{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
algebra is seen from

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{\sigma}

\displaystyle=-\mathrm{d}V\wedge\Sigma V^{-1}-V\mathrm{d}\Sigma V^{-1}+V\Sigma\wedge\mathrm{d}V^{-1}=

\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}V\Sigma\wedge\Sigma V^{-1}+\frac{1}{2}V\Sigma\wedge\Sigma V^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}V\Sigma\wedge\Sigma V^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\sigma}\wedge\tilde{\sigma},

where we have dropped the superscript but
h_{i}^{V}
are the only unit quaternions appearing.
Similarly,

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\tilde{\Sigma}

\displaystyle=\mathrm{d}V\wedge\varpi V^{-1}+V\mathrm{d}\varpi V^{-1}-V\varpi\wedge\mathrm{d}V^{-1}=

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}V\Sigma\wedge(\sigma-\Sigma)V^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}V(\sigma\wedge\sigma-\Sigma\wedge\Sigma)V^{-1}+\frac{1}{2}V(\sigma-\Sigma)\wedge\Sigma V^{-1}=

\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}V(\sigma-\Sigma)\wedge(\sigma-\Sigma)V^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}\tilde{\Sigma}\wedge\tilde{\Sigma}.

The spin connection and curvature

Now, we derive expressions for the spin connection, Riemann tensor, Ricci tensor and curvature scalar, starting from the metric
equation

5.9

\mathrm{d}s^{2}=\mathrm{d}\mu^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\sin^{2}{\mu}\>\|\varpi\|^{2}+\frac{1}{4}\lambda^{2}\|\nu+\cos\mu\>\varpi\|^{2}.

(5.13)

From this metric, we see that an orthonormal frame is provided by

e^{\hat{\imath}}=\frac{1}{2}\lambda\bigl(\nu^{i}+\cos\mu\>\varpi^{i}\bigr),\qquad e^{0}=\mathrm{d}\mu,\qquad e^{i}=\frac{1}{2}\sin{\mu}\>\varpi^{i},

(5.14)

where we have split the seven-dimensional index as
a=(\hat{\imath},0,i)
.
Note that, from a covariant perspective, the index on the first
e
should be
i
due to the right-hand side.
However, in the index split, we need to distinguish between
i
and
\hat{\imath}
.
Therefore, the notation is not completely covariant and, to avoid confusion, we will only use indices
\hat{\imath},\hat{\jmath},\hat{k},\ldots
on seven-dimensional objects and not on the
{\mathrm{SU}}(2)
-invariants
\epsilon_{ijk}
and
\delta_{ij}
.

(5.15)

To determine
\omega
, we first have to compute
\mathrm{d}e^{a}
.
To this end, we compute
\mathrm{d}\nu^{i}
and
\mathrm{d}\varpi^{i}
using

\displaystyle\nu^{i}\wedge\nu^{j}+\varpi^{i}\wedge\varpi^{j}

\displaystyle=2\bigl(\sigma^{i}\wedge\sigma^{j}+\Sigma^{i}\wedge\Sigma^{j}\bigr),

(5.16a)

\displaystyle\nu^{i}\wedge\varpi^{j}+\varpi^{i}\wedge\nu^{j}

\displaystyle=2\bigl(\sigma^{i}\wedge\sigma^{j}-\Sigma^{i}\wedge\Sigma^{j}\bigr),

(5.16b)

and express the results in terms of
e^{a}
by inverting
equation

5.14
,

\varpi^{i}=\frac{2}{\sin\mu}e^{i},\qquad\nu^{i}=-2\cot\mu\>e^{i}+\frac{2}{\lambda}e^{\hat{\imath}}.

(5.17)

\sigma
and
\Sigma

{\mathfrak{su}}(2)

, are

R_{00}=3\Bigl(1-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\Bigr),\qquad R_{ij}=3\Bigl(1-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{2}\Bigr)\delta_{ij},\qquad R_{\hat{\imath}\hat{\jmath}}=\Bigl(\lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{2\lambda^{2}}\Bigr)\delta_{ij}.

(5.23)

Finally, the curvature scalar is

R=\frac{3}{2}\Bigl(8-2\lambda^{2}+\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}\Bigr).

(5.24)

Note that, for sufficiently large
\lambda^{2}
, the curvature scalar is negative.

The Ricci tensor is diagonal in the basis we have chosen.
In particular, we see that the manifold is Einstein if and only if
\lambda^{2}=1
or
\lambda^{2}=1/5
.
The
\lambda^{2}=1
solution corresponds to the ordinary round
S^{7}

[
19
]
while
\lambda^{2}=1/5
corresponds to what we will call the Einstein-squashed or simply
the
squashed seven-sphere.

5.2
Coset construction with arbitrary squashing

As mentioned above, the squashed seven-sphere can be isometrically embedded in
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}
.
More precisely, it can be realised as a distance-sphere, that is, as all points at a fixed distance from an origin, in
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}
for squashing parameters in the range
0<\lambda^{2}\leq 1

[
19
]
.
This realisation provides insight into the isometry group of the squashed sphere.
In suitable inhomogeneous coordinates on
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}
, one finds that left-multiplication by quaternionic unitary
2\times 2
matrices and right-multiplication by unit quaternions leave both the metric of
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}
and the embedding equation invariant
[
19
]
.
Thus, the isometry group of the squashed sphere contains
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\cdot{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)
as a subgroup, where
{\mathrm{Sp}}(n)\simeq{\mathrm{U}}(n,\mathbb{H})
is the compact real form of
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2n,\mathbb{C})
, isomorphic to the quaternionic unitary group.
100
100

100

Here
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\cdot{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)={\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)/\mathbb{Z}_{2}
where
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
is the diagonal subgroup of the centre. This comes from the fact that left-multiplication by
\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1)
and right-multiplication by
-1
are equivalent.

Note that, by well-known exceptional isomorphisms
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\simeq{\mathrm{Spin}}(5)
and
{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)\simeq{\mathrm{Spin}}(3)
.
The group
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\cdot{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)\subset{\mathrm{SO}}(8)
acts transitively and effectively on the squashed sphere, whence the latter is a homogeneous space.

In this section, we use the theory from
section

4.1
to construct the squashed
S^{7}
, with arbitrary squashing parameter, as a coset.
As prescribed in
section

4.1
, we work with spin groups, that is,
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)\subset{\mathrm{Spin}}(8)
, since the manifold is spin, although we will almost exclusively be concerned with the Lie algebras.

If we denote the (lifted) group of isometries by
G={\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{C}
and break
{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)
to
{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{A}\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{B}\simeq{\mathrm{Spin}}(4)
(corresponding to fixing a
{\mathrm{SO}}(5)
-vector), the isotropy subgroup of
G
is
H={\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{A}\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{B+C}
, where
{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{B+C}
denotes the diagonal subgroup of
{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{B}\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{C}
.
Again, this is seen from the embedding in
\mathbb{H}\mathbf{P}^{2}

[
19
]
.
Thus, the squashed seven-sphere, with any squashing parameter
0<\lambda^{2}\leq 1
, is isometric to the coset space

\frac{G}{H}=\frac{{\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{C}}{{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{A}\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{B+C}},

(5.25)

with an appropriate metric.
We will now demonstrate this in detail and find that this is the case even for
\lambda^{2}>1
.
The construction is similar to that of
[
20
]
but we generalise it to an arbitrary squashing parameter.

The metric

As explained in
section

4.1
, we need an
\mathfrak{h}
-invariant symmetric tensor
g_{ab}
to construct the metric on the coset (
g_{ab}
is the metric with flat indices).
By using, for instance,
[
106
,
107
]
one finds that the
{\mathfrak{so}}(7)
-representation
\bm{7}^{\odot 2}\simeq\bm{1}\oplus\bm{27}
contains two
\mathfrak{h}
-singlets.
101
101

101

The decomposition of the relevant
{\mathfrak{so}}(7)
-representations can also be found in
[
10
]
.

Two is also the number of simple factors in
\mathfrak{g}
whence there are two
\mathfrak{g}
-invariants
g^{(1)}_{AB}
and
g^{(2)}_{AB}
corresponding to the two quadratic Casimirs of
\mathfrak{g}
.
Hence, all
G
-invariant metrics on the coset are of normal homogeneous form.
102
102

102

This is not entirely true in the strict sense of
section

4.1
since the
\mathfrak{g}
-invariant may not be of Euclidean signature. Also, there can be exceptions in degenerate cases.

To get a metric on the coset, we, therefore, start by finding the invariants
g^{(n)}_{AB}
.
To this end, we compute all commutators and the Cartan–Killing metric of
\mathfrak{g}
and then relate the latter to the invariants via the Casimirs of
{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)
and
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}
.

To make everything explicit but not lose generality, we work in a faithful representation.
Recall that
\gamma
-matrices of
{\mathfrak{so}}(5)
can be constructed by joining
\gamma^{5}
to the
\gamma
-matrices of
{\mathfrak{so}}(4)
.
We use the tensor product of the spinor representation of
{\mathfrak{so}}(5)\simeq{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)
and the 2-dimensional spinor representation of
{\mathfrak{so}}(3)\simeq{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}
.
Thus, the generators can be written as

\displaystyle T^{(A)}_{i}=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{i}&0\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes\mathds{1}_{2},\quad\ T^{(B)}_{i}=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&\sigma_{i}\end{pmatrix}\otimes\mathds{1}_{2},\quad\ T^{(C)}_{i}=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\mathds{1}_{4}\otimes\sigma_{i}

\displaystyle T^{(Q)}_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0&-\mathds{1}_{2}\\
\mathds{1}_{2}&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes\mathds{1}_{2},\qquad T^{(Q)}_{i}=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma_{i}\\
\sigma_{i}&0\end{pmatrix}\otimes\mathds{1}_{2},

(5.26)

where the labels
A,B,C
indicate which
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)
algebra the generators belong to,
T^{(Q)}
are the remaining generators,
\mathds{1}_{n}
is the
n\times n
unit matrix and
\sigma_{i}
are the Pauli matrices.
To see this, note that the
\gamma
-matrices of
{\mathfrak{so}}(4)
can be obtained from those of
{\mathfrak{so}}(3,1)
by multiplying
\gamma^{0}
by
\mathrm{i}
.
The generators of
{\mathfrak{so}}(3,1)
, which are proportional to
\gamma^{\alpha\beta}
, are block-diagonal in the Weyl-basis of
section

B.3
.
The blocks in these six generators are
\mathrm{i}\sigma^{i}
and by appropriate linear combinations,
T^{(A)}_{i}
and
T^{(B)}_{i}
can be obtained.
103
103

103

Note that we use the convention in which a group element is
g=\exp(T)
.

This explicitly demonstrates the well-known exceptional isomorphisms
{\mathfrak{so}}(4)\simeq{\mathfrak{su}}(2)\oplus{\mathfrak{su}}(2)
.
The last generators of
{\mathfrak{so}}(5)
are proportional to
\gamma^{\alpha 5}
and are the ones denoted
T^{(Q)}
above.
The normalisations of the three commuting
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)
algebras are such that
[T_{i},T_{j}]=\mathchoice{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scripts \displaystyle\bigl[T^{(Q)}_{i},T^{(Q)}_{0}\bigr]=T^{(A)}_{i}-T^{(B)}_{i},\qquad

\displaystyle\bigl[T^{(Q)}_{i},T^{(Q)}_{j}\bigr]=\mathchoice{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{k}}}_{{{i}{j}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.42017pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.7052pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.93228pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\epsilon^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$ (5.27c)

From these commutation relations, it is easy to see that the Cartan–Killing metric
\kappa_{AB}=f_{AC}{}^{D}f_{BD}{}^{C}
, where
A,B,C,\ldots
are
\mathfrak{g}
-indices, is block diagonal in our basis.
For instance, the
(A),(Q)
-block vanishes since
T^{(A)}
only has nonvanishing brackets
[T^{(A)},T^{(A)}]\sim T^{(A)}
and
[T^{(A)},T^{(Q)}]\sim T^{(Q)}
while
[T^{(Q)},T^{(A)}]
has no
T^{(A)}
part and
[T^{(Q)},T^{(Q)}]
has no
T^{(Q)}
part.
A short calculation gives,

\kappa_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(-3\cdot\mathds{1}_{3},-3\cdot\mathds{1}_{3},-2\cdot\mathds{1}_{3},-6\cdot\mathds{1}_{4})_{AB},

(5.28)

where we have ordered the generators as
(T^{(A)},T^{(B)},T^{(C)},T^{(Q)})
.

We define the quadratic Casimir of
\mathfrak{g}
by

\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}=6\kappa^{AB}T_{A}T_{B}.

(5.29)

Since
\mathfrak{g}={\mathfrak{sp}}(2)\oplus{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}
,
\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}
is a linear combination of
\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)}
and
\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}}
.
To find the coefficients, we compute
\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}})
.
From the definition, we immediately find that
\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}})
is
6\cdot\mathds{1}_{3}
on the
(C)
-block, that is, the
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}
part.
After a short calculation, we find that
\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{g}}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}})
is
6\cdot\mathds{1}_{3}
on the
(A)
-block as well, whence it is
6\cdot\mathds{1}_{10}
on the
{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)
part by Shur’s lemma.
With the normalisation of the Casimirs from
section

A.3
, we conclude that

\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}=2\,\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)}+3\,\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}},

(5.30)

since
C_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)}(\operatorname{ad}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)})=3
and
C_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)}(\operatorname{ad}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)})=2
and
\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{g}}=\operatorname{ad}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)}\oplus\operatorname{ad}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}}
.
104
104

104

We use
\mathcal{C}
to denote the Casimir operators and
C
for its eigenvalues.

The Casimirs
\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)}
and
\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}}
can be written as

\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}}=-g_{(1)}^{AB}T_{A}T_{B},\qquad\quad\mathcal{C}_{{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)}=-g_{(2)}^{AB}T_{A}T_{B},

(5.31)

where
g_{(1)}^{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(0,0,\mathds{1}_{3},0)^{AB}
and
g_{(2)}^{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathds{1}_{3},\mathds{1}_{3},0,\mathds{1}_{4}/2)^{AB}
are
\mathfrak{g}
-invariant tensors.
From these, we can form the invariants

g^{(1)}_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(0,\,0,\,\mathds{1}_{3},\,0)_{AB},\qquad g^{(2)}_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathds{1}_{3},\,\mathds{1}_{3},\,0,\,2\cdot\mathds{1}_{4})_{AB}.

(5.32)

Note that
g^{(n)}_{AB}
is not the inverse of
g_{(n)}^{AB}
.
Rather,
P^{(n)}{}_{\mkern-8.0muA}^{\,C}=g^{(n)}_{AB}g_{(n)}^{BC}
, for
n=1,2
, are the projection operators onto
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}
and
{\mathfrak{sp}}(2)
, respectively.
Since there are two simple factors in
\mathfrak{g}
, these span the space of
\mathfrak{g}
-invariants
g_{AB}
.

We now write the
\mathfrak{g}
-invariant that we will use to define the metric on the coset as

g_{AB}=\frac{1}{2\sin(\theta)}\bigl(\cos\theta\,g^{(1)}_{AB}+\sin\theta\,g^{(2)}_{AB}\bigr),

(5.33)

where
\theta
is referred to as the squashing angle for reasons that will soon become apparent.
Apart from an overall constant factor, which is irrelevant for the geometry, this is an arbitrary
\mathfrak{g}
-invariant except that we have to exclude
\theta=0
due to the prefactor.
We need only consider half a revolution for the squashing angle since
\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi
leaves
g_{AB}
invariant.
At this point, we thus have two relevant regions
0<\theta<\pi/2
and
\pi/2<\theta<\pi
in which
g_{AB}
is of signature
(13,0)
, that is, Euclidean, and
(10,3)
, respectively, as well as the midpoint
\theta=\pi/2
in which
g_{AB}
is degenerate.
As we will see, this will change when we go over to the metric on the coset.

Following
section

4.1
, we now wish to split
\mathfrak{g}
into a direct sum
\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{m}
such that
[\mathfrak{h},\mathfrak{m}]\subseteq\mathfrak{m}
and
g_{AB}
is block-diagonal over the terms.
At the same time, we will switch to a basis in which
g_{ab}=\delta_{ab}
, where
g_{ab}
is the restriction of
g_{AB}
to
\mathfrak{m}
(we use
a,b,c\ldots
for
\mathfrak{m}
-indices).
To this end, we write the generators of
\mathfrak{g}
as

\displaystyle\mathfrak{h}\colon\qquad

\displaystyle T^{(A)}_{i},\qquad

\displaystyle T^{(B+C)}_{i}=T^{(B)}_{i}+T^{(C)}_{i},

(5.34a)

\displaystyle\mathfrak{m}\colon\qquad

\displaystyle T^{(Q)}_{\alpha},\qquad

\displaystyle T^{(T)}_{i}=f(\theta)T^{(B)}_{i}-\tan\theta\,f(\theta)T^{(C)}_{i},

(5.34b)

where

f(\theta)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{1+\tan{\theta}}}.

(5.35)

Note that
T^{(B+C)}_{i}
generate
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{B+C}
, the diagonal subalgebra of
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{B}\oplus{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{C}
.
Here, we need to exclude the region in which
\tan\theta\leq-1
and
\theta=\pi/2
where
\tan\theta
diverges.
In the new basis for
\mathfrak{g}
,

g_{AB}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathds{1}_{3}/2,\,(1+\cot\theta)\mathds{1}_{3}/2,\,\mathds{1}_{7})_{AB},

(5.36)

where the index
A
is split as
A=(R,a)
where
R
is an
\mathfrak{h}
-index and
a
an
\mathfrak{m}
-index.
The index
R
is further split as
R=(r,\dot{r})
corresponding to the terms in
\mathfrak{h}={\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{A}\oplus{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)_{B+C}
.
The metric in
equation

5.36
is computed from
equations

5.32
and
5.33
by matrix multiplication,
g^{\prime}_{AB}=M_{A}{}^{C}M_{B}{}^{D}g_{CD}
, where
M_{A}{}^{B}
is the matrix relating the two bases,
T^{\prime}_{A}=M_{A}{}^{B}T_{B}
.
Note that the split
\mathfrak{h}\oplus\mathfrak{m}
is reductive since
g_{AB}
is
\mathfrak{g}
-invariant which implies that
f_{AB}{}^{D}g_{DC}
is completely antisymmetric whence
f_{Sa}{}^{T}=0
follows from
g_{AB}
being invertible and
\mathfrak{h}
being a subalgebra of
\mathfrak{g}
.

Before we turn to the Riemann and Ricci tensors, some comments about the range of values of
\theta
.
Due to
\tan\theta<-1
being excluded and
\theta\sim\theta+\pi
, it is convenient to consider
\theta
in the interval
-\pi/4<\theta<\pi/2
.
The quotient between the coefficients of
T^{(B)}
and
T^{(C)}
in
T^{(T)}
are determined by requiring
g_{AB}
to be diagonal in the new basis while the factor
f(\theta)
and the prefactor in
equation

5.33
ensures
g_{ab}=\delta_{ab}
.
Since there are two
\mathfrak{h}
-invariants
g_{ab}^{(1),(2)}
, we conclude that
-\pi/4<\theta<\pi/2
corresponds to linear combinations of these such that the result has signature
(7,0)
, that is, Euclidean, while
\pi/2<\theta<3\pi/4
corresponds to signature
(4,3)
.
Similarly, the points
\theta=-\pi/4,\,\pi/2
corresponds to degenerate linear combinations.
This situation is precisely what one expects from there being two
\mathfrak{h}
-invariants
g^{(1),(2)}_{ab}
.
Recall, however, that we also had to exclude
\theta=0
.
Without the diverging prefactor in
equation

5.33
,
g_{AB}
would only have rank 3 for
\theta=0
.
Clearly, such a
g_{AB}
cannot be restricted to a nondegenerate metric on
\mathfrak{h}
.
However, it seems like
\theta=0
will not be problematic when we forget about
g_{AB}
and only consider the coset since the divergences sit in
g_{RS}
, not
g_{ab}
, and there is no singularity in the basis in
equation

5.34
at
\theta=0
.
This agrees with the above remark that the
\mathfrak{h}
-metric is degenerate for
\theta=-\pi/4,\,\pi/2
, not
\theta=0
.
Note that the coset is Euclidean even when
g_{AB}
is non-Euclidean (but nondegenerate) as long as
T^{(B+C)}_{i}
are time-like.
The problematic
\theta=-\pi/4
corresponds to light-like
T^{(B+C)}_{i}
.

The Riemann and Ricci tensors

To compute the Riemann tensor, we use
equation

4.15
.
Thus, we first need to compute the structure constants in the basis in
equation

5.34
.
We use the index split
A=(R,a)=(r,\dot{r},a)
described above and further split
a
as
a=(\hat{\imath},0,i)
, where
T_{\hat{\imath}}=T^{(T)}_{\hat{\imath}}
,
T_{0}=T^{(Q)}_{0}
and
T_{i}=T^{(Q)}_{i}
.

Since
T^{(C)}_{i}
commute with everything else, all commutators are easily computed using the
{\mathfrak{sp}}(1)
commutation relations and
equation

5.27
.
We find that the nonvanishing components are

6.   Eigenvalue spectra of the squashed seven-sphere

In this chapter, we derive the eigenvalue spectra of the universal Laplacian of the squashed seven-sphere.
We will only consider the Einstein-squashed sphere and, henceforth, refer to it simply as the squashed
S^{7}
.
We will consider eigenmodes of the Laplacian,
\Delta
, from
section

3.2.4
and use
equation

4.36
to determine the possible eigenvalues.
As mentioned in
section

1.1
, the spectra of all operators we consider except
\mathrm{i}\not{\mathcal{D}}_{3/2}
are already known
[
22
,
23
,
19
,
21
]
.

On a high level, the derivation goes as follows.
First, assume that we have an eigenmode of
\Delta
with some eigenvalue
\kappa^{2}
.
Since, as explained in
section

4.3
, the eigenmodes of
\Delta
fall into irreducible representations of
G={\mathrm{Sp}}(2)\times{\mathrm{Sp}}(1)_{C}
,
\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}
can be replaced by its corresponding eigenvalue
C_{\mathfrak{g}}
on the relevant representation.
We will not investigate which irreducible
G
-representations occur in the
G
-representation induced by the relevant irreducible
H
-representations.
It has, however, been done using Young tableaux techniques
[
10
]
.
Replacing
\Delta
by
\kappa^{2}
and
\mathcal{C}_{\mathfrak{g}}
by
C_{\mathfrak{g}}
, we are left with a linear map that acts on the spin-index of the mode in the right-hand side of
equation

4.36
.
In the left-hand side, however, we have a first-order differential operator.
To get rid of this, we will use various techniques, such as squaring it, acting with projection operators and combinations thereof.
This will, eventually, result in a polynomial equation for
\kappa^{2}
.

In general, there can be false roots, that is, solutions to the polynomial equation that are not actual eigenvalues of
\Delta
.
We will not deal with this in the current chapter.
Note, however, that, as long as we do not introduce any assumptions in the derivation, as we will not,
\kappa^{2}
being an eigenvalue of
\Delta

implies
that it is a root of the polynomial.
Thus, although we can get false roots, we cannot miss any eigenvalues.

In
chapter

5
, we used a dimensionless unit system such that, for Einstein-squashing,

(6.1)

m^{2}=\frac{9}{20}.

(6.2)

Here, we will mostly continue to use the dimensionless system for convenience.
Note, however, that there is a sign choice in

6.2

In this chapter, we only concern ourselves with operators on the squashed seven-sphere.
The sign choice will become important in
chapter

7

(6.10)

Since

,
a_{abc}(T_{i})^{bc}=0
.

\bm{21}
to
\bm{7}
while

to

.
Similarly,

, whence also

.

6.6
Spinors

Now that we have dealt with all tensorial representations, we turn to the spinorial ones, starting with the spinors.
Thus, consider a spinor satisfying

\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}Y_{a}
using the scalar equation,

\frac{9}{20}C_{\mathfrak{g}}Y=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{5}}\Bigl(C_{\mathfrak{g}}-\kappa^{2}+\frac{9}{20}\Bigl)\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}Y_{a}=\Bigl(C_{\mathfrak{g}}-\kappa^{2}+\frac{9}{20}\Bigl)\Bigl(C_{\mathfrak{g}}-\kappa^{2}+\frac{63}{20}\Bigl)Y.

(6.80)

Thus, either
\kappa^{2}
is given by
equation

6.82a
below or
Y=0
.
In the latter case,
\check{\mathcal{D}}^{a}Y_{a}=0
, that is,
Y_{a}
is a transverse 1-form, by the scalar equation and the vector equation becomes

\mathfrak{D}_{1}Y_{a}=-2\sqrt{5}\Bigl(C_{\mathfrak{g}}-\kappa^{2}+\frac{3}{20}\Bigl)Y_{a}.

(6.81)

This situation is identical to that in
section

6.2
apart from numerical constants.
Reusing that calculation gives
equation

6.82b
.
Thus,

\displaystyle\kappa^{2}=C_{\mathfrak{g}}+\frac{9}{5}\pm\frac{3}{2\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{C_{\mathfrak{g}}+\frac{81}{20}},

(6.82a)

\displaystyle\kappa^{2}=C_{\mathfrak{g}}+\frac{1}{10}\pm\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\sqrt{C_{\mathfrak{g}}+\frac{49}{20}},

(6.82b)

where the top row applies to modes with nonzero scalar part,
\bar{\eta}\psi\neq 0
, and the second otherwise.

6.7
Vector-spinors

Lastly, we turn to transverse
\Gamma
-traceless vector-spinors.
These carry the representation
\bm{48}
of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(7)
which splits into
\bm{7}\oplus\bm{14}\oplus\bm{27}
when restricted to
G_{2}
.
We consider an eigenmode
\psi_{a}
of
\Delta
with eigenvalue
\kappa^{2}
.
The transversality and
\Gamma
-tracelessness conditions are
\mathcal{D}^{a}\psi_{a}=0
and
\Gamma^{a}\psi_{a}=0
, respectively.
The
{\mathfrak{so}}(7)
-Casimir is
C_{{\mathfrak{so}}(7)}(\bm{48})=49/8
, whence the rewritten quadratic master equation,
equation

6.13
, becomes

\mathchoice{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}{c}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}{c}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}{c}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}{c}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][
