.

Arbitrary products of
\Gamma
-matrices can be computed by combinatorics.
This is most easily seen in a basis in which
\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,\dots,-1,1,\dots,1)
but is valid in any basis, as long as the results are written in a basis-independent way, and follows directly from
equation

B.1
.
The simplification comes from the fact that, in this basis,
\Gamma^{a}
squares to
\pm\mathds{1}
and
\Gamma^{a_{1}\dots a_{n}}=\Gamma^{a_{1}}\dots\Gamma^{a_{n}}
as long as the indices are distinct.
As an example, consider
\Gamma^{ab}\Gamma_{cd}
.
Here, either all indices are distinct (1 possibility); one of
a
,
b
coincides with one of
c
,
d
(4 possibilities) or both of
a
,
b
coincide with one of
c
,
d
each (2 possibilities).
Thus,

\Gamma^{ab}\Gamma_{cd}=\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.55038pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.8217pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}{d}}}}{\Gamma^{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.55038pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.8217pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}{d}}}}{\Gamma^{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.55038pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.8217pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}{d}}}}{\Gamma^{{{a}{b}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.57375pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1205pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.51463pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.16287pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.55038pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.8217pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{c}{d}}}}-4\delta^{[a}_{[c}\mathchoice{\Gamma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\Gamma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\Gamma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\Gamma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}-2\delta^{ab}_{cd}\mathds{1},

(B.4)

where the signs come from anticommuting
\Gamma
-matrices with distinct indices.
This can be generalised to cases with contracted indices and more than two factors.
For instance,
\Gamma^{a}\Gamma_{a}=d\mathds{1}
and

\Gamma_{b}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}}\Gamma^{b}=(-1)^{n}(d-2n)\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}}.

(B.5)

In the latter, there are
d-n
values of
b
that do not coincide with any of the
a
’s and
n
values of
b
that coincide with one of the
a
’s.
These identities can be used to see that

d\operatorname{tr}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}}=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma^{b}\Gamma_{b}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}})=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma_{b}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}}\Gamma^{b})=(-1)^{n}(d-2n)\operatorname{tr}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}},

(B.6)

which implies that
\operatorname{tr}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}}=0
if
n\neq 0
and, for odd
d
,
n\neq d
.

B.1
Spinors in arbitrary even dimension

Let us, for a moment, consider the case of even dimension,
d=r+s=2k
.
The dimension of the Dirac spinor representation is
2^{k}

[
73
]
.
A basis of
\operatorname{End}(V_{S},V_{S})
, that is,
2^{k}\times 2^{k}
matrices after a choice of basis for the Dirac representation space
V_{S}
, is provided by
\mathds{1},\Gamma^{a_{1}},\ldots,\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}
when restricted to antisymmetrically independent index combinations.
To see this, consider

X=\sum_{i=0}^{d}x_{a_{1}\ldots a_{i}}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{i}},

(B.7)

where all
x_{a_{1}\ldots a_{i}}
are completely antisymmetric.
From the above remarks on how to compute products and traces of
\Gamma
-matrices, we see that
x_{a_{1}\ldots a_{i}}\propto\operatorname{tr}(X\Gamma_{a_{1}\ldots a_{i}})
.
Thus,
X=0
implies that all the
x
’s are 0, whence we have established linear independence.
By counting, we now see that there are
2^{d}=2^{k}\cdot 2^{k}
linearly independent components of
X
, which is precisely the dimension of
\operatorname{End}(V_{S},V_{S})
.

Chirality and Weyl spinors

Since there is only one antisymmetrically independent index combination with
d
indices, we may define
\gamma
by
123
123

123

In
d=4
, this is commonly denoted by
\gamma^{5}
.

\gamma\epsilon^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}=i^{k+s}\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}.

(B.8)

It is easy to see that
\gamma^{2}=\mathds{1}
and
\{\gamma,\Gamma^{a}\}=0
.
Note that
(\Gamma^{a})_{A}{}^{B}
, where
A,B
are Dirac spinor indices, is a
{\mathfrak{so}}(r,s)
-invariant, as seen from

L_{ab}\cdot(\Gamma^{c})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=\frac{1}{4}(\Gamma_{ab}\Gamma^{c})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}-\frac{1}{4}(\Gamma^{c}\Gamma_{ab})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}+\delta_{ab}^{cd}(\Gamma_{d})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=0.

(B.9)

Thus,
\gamma
is also an invariant and the Dirac spinor representation is reducible by Shur’s lemma since
\gamma
is not proportional to
\mathds{1}
.
We may form projection operators

P_{\pm}=\frac{\mathds{1}\pm\gamma}{2},

(B.10)

projecting onto the invariant subspaces with
\gamma
-eigenvalue
\pm 1
, respectively.
These smaller dimensional representations are known as the left and right-handed Weyl spinor representations.
Note that, if
\gamma\Psi=\pm\Psi
, then
\gamma\Gamma^{a}\Psi=\mp\Gamma^{a}\Psi
, that is,
\Gamma^{a}
interchanges left and right-handed spinor.
Thus, writing a Dirac spinor as
\Psi_{A}=(\psi_{\alpha},\chi^{\tilde{\alpha}})_{A}
, where
\psi
and
\chi
are Weyl spinors of the two kinds, this implies that

(\Gamma^{a})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&(\Gamma^{a})_{\alpha\tilde{\beta}}\\
(\Gamma^{a})^{\tilde{\alpha}\beta}&0\end{pmatrix}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.6806pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.6806pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34169pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.29169pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{{\mkern-6.0mu}A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}},

(B.11)

where we have introduced chiral
\Gamma
-matrices.
In this basis, we see explicitly that the Dirac spinor representation of
{\mathfrak{so}}(r,s)
is reducible since
\Gamma^{ab}
is block-diagonal.
For even
d
, one can prove that there is only one irreducible representation of the Clifford algebra and that the Weyl spinor representations of
{\mathfrak{so}}(r,s)
are irreducible
[
73
]
.

Invariant tensors and Majorana spinors

There are a few other invariants apart from
\gamma
.
To see this, note that we can construct a new set of matrices satisfying
equation

B.1
by taking the negative, complex conjugate, transpose or any combination thereof of all matrices
\Gamma^{a}
.
Consider first the negative.
Since there is only one inequivalent irreducible Clifford algebra representation, there exists a matrix
M_{A}{}^{B}
such that
-\Gamma^{a}=M\Gamma^{a}M^{-1}
, relating the two representations.
Note that this equation is linear in
M
, which is seen by writing it as
M\Gamma^{a}=-\Gamma^{a}M
.
The space of solutions is one-dimensional by Shur’s lemma.
From the above, we see that
M=\gamma
provides a canonical choice of
M
.

Similarly, there are two one-dimensional spaces of solutions
(B_{\pm})_{\bar{A}}{}^{B}
to

B_{\pm}\Gamma^{a}=\pm(\Gamma^{a})^{\ast}B_{\pm}.

(B.12)

These two spaces are related by
B_{-}=B_{+}\gamma
.
Taking the complex conjugate of
equation

B.12
, we find that
(B_{\pm}^{\ast})^{-1}
are also solutions whence
(B_{\pm}^{\ast})^{-1}=z_{\pm}B_{\pm}
for some
z_{\pm}\in\mathbb{C}
.
Complex conjugating this relation, we find
z_{\pm}\in\mathbb{R}
.
Since the left and right-handed spinor representations are inequivalent,
124
124

124

Note that
\gamma\propto\epsilon_{a_{1}b_{1}\ldots a_{k}b_{k}}\Gamma^{a_{1}b_{1}}\ldots\Gamma^{a_{k}b_{k}}
is a
k
’th-order Casimir with different eigenvalue on the two Weyl representations.

B_{\pm}
are either block diagonal or block antidiagonal in the Weyl basis,
\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(\mathds{1},-\mathds{1})
.
With
B_{-}=B_{+}\gamma
, we find that
z_{-}=\pm z_{+}
in the two cases, respectively.
By rescaling
B_{\pm}
,
z_{\pm}
is rescaled by a positive real number whence we may scale
B_{\pm}
such that
z_{\pm}\in\set{-1,+1}
while maintaining
B_{-}=B_{+}\gamma
.

Due to the index structure of
B
, we may ask whether there are any solutions to
\psi=B^{-1}\psi^{\ast}
.
To this end, define the antilinear (conjugate-linear) map
R\colon V_{S}\to V_{S}
by
\psi\mapsto B^{-1}\psi^{\ast}
.
Squaring this gives

R^{2}(\psi)=R(B^{-1}\psi^{\ast})=B^{-1}(B^{\ast})^{-1}\psi=z\psi,

(B.13)

where
z=\pm 1
after the above rescaling of
B
.
Consider first
z=+1
so that
R^{2}
is the identity map.
We claim that there is a basis in which
B
coincides numerically with the unit matrix, which motivates the notation
B_{\bar{A}}{}^{B}=\delta_{\bar{A}}^{B}
.
To see this, pick any
\psi
and let
\chi=R(\psi)
.
Suppose that
\psi
and
\chi
are linearly dependent so that
\chi=c\psi
for some constant
c
.
By antilinearity and
R^{2}=\mathds{1}
,
\psi=R(\chi)=\bar{c}\chi=|c|^{2}\psi
whence
c=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}
.
Now, with
\psi^{\prime}=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\varphi}\psi
,
R(\psi^{\prime})=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\theta-2\varphi)}\psi^{\prime}
.
Thus, for an appropriate choice of
\varphi
, we get
R(\psi^{\prime})=\psi^{\prime}
.
Taking
\psi^{\prime}
as our first basis vector,
B
becomes block diagonal with a
1
in the upper left corner.
If, on the other hand,
\psi
and
\chi
are linearly independent, we find

R(\psi+\chi)=\chi+\psi,\qquad R(\mathrm{i}\psi-\mathrm{i}\chi)=-\mathrm{i}\chi+\mathrm{i}\psi.

(B.14)

In this case, we get two basis vectors,
\psi+\chi
and
\mathrm{i}\psi-\mathrm{i}\chi
, which are mapped to themselves by
R
.
Proceeding by induction, we conclude that there is a basis such that
B
is diagonal with
1
s on the diagonal.
Since
B\Gamma^{a}=\pm(\Gamma^{a})^{\ast}B
, the
\Gamma
-matrices are real (
+
) or imaginary (
-
) in this basis.
In both cases, the generators of
{\mathfrak{so}}(p,q)
are real.
Furthermore,
\psi=R(\psi)
reduces to the condition that the components of
\psi
are real.
This is known as a Majorana basis and the reality condition,
\psi=R(\psi)
, is the Majorana condition.
If
B
is block diagonal in the Weyl basis, we can define Majorana–Weyl spinors by requiring both
\gamma\psi=\pm\psi
and
R(\psi)=\psi
.
If
B
is block antidiagonal, the Majorana condition gives a relation between the left and right-handed components and there are no Majorana–Weyl spinors.
In the above,
B
is only well-defined up to a global complex phase.
If
B
is redefined by
B\mapsto\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta}B
, the real subspace defined by the Majorana condition is rotated by
\theta/2
.

In the case
z=-1
, there is clearly no solution to
\psi=R(\psi)
whence it is not possible to define Majorana spinors.
However, given two Dirac spinors
\psi
and
\chi
, one may impose the relation
\chi=R(\psi)
, known as the symplectic Majorana condition.
125
125

125

When considering Grassmann-odd spinors, there is another generalisation of the Majorana condition, the graded Majorana condition, which can be imposed on a single Dirac spinor
[
109
]
.

In this case,
R
can be used to turn
V_{S}
into a quaternionic space by defining
\mathrm{j}\psi=R(\psi)
.
126
126

126

Since
R
is antilinear,
\mathrm{i}\mathrm{j}=-\mathrm{j}\mathrm{i}
.

This has applications in extended supersymmetry, see for instance
[
110
]
.

There are also invariants
(A_{\pm})^{\bar{A}B}
and
(C_{\pm})^{AB}
satisfying

A_{\pm}\Gamma^{a}=\pm(\Gamma^{a})^{\dagger}A_{\pm},\qquad\quad C_{\pm}\Gamma^{a}=\pm(\Gamma^{a})^{\mathrm{T}}C_{\pm}.

(B.15)

Note that these equations are linear in
A
and
C
whence there are one-dimensional spaces of solutions.
Again, the different signs can be related by
A_{-}=A_{+}\gamma
and
C_{-}=C_{+}\gamma
.
There is also a relation
A\propto(B^{-1})^{\mathrm{T}}C
, as seen from the index structure or a straightforward calculation.
By defining the Dirac conjugate
\bar{\psi}=\psi^{\dagger}A
and the Majorana conjugate
\tilde{\psi}=\psi^{\mathrm{T}}C
, we find that the relation
A=(B^{-1})^{\mathrm{T}}C
is necessary for the Majorana condition
\psi=B^{-1}\psi^{\ast}
to take its usual form
\bar{\psi}=\tilde{\psi}
.

It is easy to see that
A_{\pm}^{\dagger}
also satisfies
equation

B.15
, whence
A_{\pm}^{\dagger}\propto A_{\pm}
.
When
A
is rescaled, the phase of the proportionality constant changes.
Thus, we can choose
A
Hermitian, which makes it well-defined up to a real constant factor.
In the case we are dealing with Majorana spinors, this is not always convenient.
In that case, instead note that
B^{\mathrm{T}}C^{\ast}B=z_{C}C_{\pm}
by an analogous argument.
With the above normalisation
(B^{\ast})^{-1}=\pm B
(with the plus sign in the Majorana case), it follows that
|z_{C}|=1
.
By rescaling
C
, we set
z_{C}=1
.
In the Majorana basis,
B=\mathds{1}
, this means that
C
is real.
Insisting that
A=(B^{-1})^{\mathrm{T}}C
, we find
A^{\dagger}=(B^{-1})^{\mathrm{T}}C^{\mathrm{T}}
.
By transposing the equation for
C
in
equation

B.15
, it is easy to see that
C^{\mathrm{T}}=\pm C
by using that the solution space is one-dimensional.
Thus,
A
is (anti-)Hermitian when
C
is (anti-)symmetric.
Again,
A
and
C
are only well-defined up to a real constant after imposing these conditions.

B.2
Spinors in arbitrary odd dimension

Consider now
d=2k+1
.
We may construct a representation of the Clifford algebra by using the
\Gamma
-matrices from
d=2k
and taking a multiple of
\gamma
as the last
\Gamma
-matrix.
By adding
\pm\gamma
to a set of
\Gamma
-matrices with signature
(r,s)
we end up with signature
(r+1,s)
.
To instead get
(r,s+1)
,
\pm\mathrm{i}\gamma
should be used as the last
\Gamma
-matrix.
Since there is only one inequivalent representation of
\mathrm{C}\mathchoice{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\displaystyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\textstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\scriptstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\scriptscriptstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}_{r,s}
but a sign choice for the last
\Gamma
-matrix when we go up in dimension, there seems to be two inequivalent representations of
\mathrm{C}\mathchoice{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\displaystyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\textstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\scriptstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\scriptscriptstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}_{r+1,s}
and
\mathrm{C}\mathchoice{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\displaystyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\textstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\scriptstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}{\mathord{\lower 0.43057pt\hbox{\kern-8.88892pt\hbox{\rotatebox{10.0}{$\scriptscriptstyle\ell$}}\kern-8.88892pt}}}_{r,s+1}
.
To see that the sign choice really gives inequivalent representations of the
d=2k+1
Clifford algebras, note that

\Gamma^{d}=c\gamma\quad\implies\quad\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}=c(-\mathrm{i})^{k+s}\epsilon^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}\mathds{1}.

(B.16)

Thus,
c
, which can take two values once the signature is fixed, distinguishes the two representations and they are indeed inequivalent.
These representations are irreducible
[
73
]
.
The inequivalent Clifford representations are related by
\Gamma^{a}\mapsto-\Gamma^{a}
.
Note that this implies that the
{\mathfrak{so}}
-representations generated by
\Gamma^{ab}/4
are the same.
Since there is no longer an invariant
\gamma
, the situation is reversed compared to even dimensions;
in odd dimensions, there are two inequivalent irreducible Clifford algebra representations but only one irreducible spinor representation, the Dirac representation.

Due to
equation

B.16
,
\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{n}}
and
\Gamma^{a_{n+1}\ldots a_{d}}
are not linearly independent but related by a contraction with
\epsilon^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}
.
Thus, a basis for
\operatorname{End}(V_{S},V_{S})
is provided by
\mathds{1},\Gamma^{a_{1}},\ldots,\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{k}}
where, in contrast to the even-dimensional case, there are at most
k
indices.
Linear independence is proved analogously to the case of even dimension.
Counting the antisymmetrically independent index combinations, we find that the span of
\mathds{1},\Gamma^{a_{1}},\ldots,\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{k}}
is
2^{2k}
-dimensional, which agrees with the dimension of
\operatorname{End}(V_{S},V_{S})
.

In odd dimension, there are only half as many invariants as in even dimension.
More specifically, only one of the signs in each of
A_{\pm}
,
B_{\pm}
and
C_{\pm}
is viable.
Since these invariants intertwine representations of the Clifford algebra, it is easy to see which of them exists by using that the inequivalent representations are distinguished by the sign of
\Gamma^{a_{1}\ldots a_{d}}
.
In
section

B.4
, we demonstrate this explicitly for
C_{\pm}
in
d=11
.

B.3
Spinors in four dimensions

In four dimensions, a Dirac spinor,
\Psi_{A}
, has four components and consists of a left-handed and a right-handed irreducible Weyl spinor,
\psi_{\alpha}
and
\bar{\chi}^{\dot{\alpha}}
.
127
127

127

Here, we use a dot instead of a bar on complex conjugated indices, as is common in Van der Waerden notation.

A chiral basis

In the chiral (Weyl) basis,
\Psi_{A}=(\psi_{\alpha},\bar{\chi}^{\dot{\alpha}})_{A}
and (note the factor of
\mathrm{i}
)

(\gamma^{a})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=\mathrm{i}\begin{pmatrix}0&\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}\\
\bar{\sigma}^{a\dot{\alpha}\beta}&0\end{pmatrix}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.6806pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.6806pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34169pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.29169pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{{\mkern-6.0mu}A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}},

(B.17)

where, in the basis we choose and with index structure
\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}
, the Pauli matrices are

\sigma^{0}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma^{1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\mathrm{i}\\
\mathrm{i}&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma^{3}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&-1\end{pmatrix}.

(B.18)

In four spacetime dimensions, there is a useful exceptional isomorphism
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,1)\simeq{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb{C})
.
This means that the Weyl spinor representation of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,1)
is the defining representation of
{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb{C})
, whence the antisymmetric tensor
\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}
is invariant.
This isomorphism is indicated by the fact that there is a one-to-one correspondence between real-valued vectors
v_{a}
and Hermitian matrices
V\coloneqq v_{a}\sigma^{a}
.
Given
V
, we can construct another Hermitian matrix
V^{\prime}
by

V^{\prime}=\Lambda\,V\Lambda^{\dagger}

(B.19)

In this transformation, a global phase of
\Lambda
is irrelevant whence we can demand
\det{\Lambda}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
.
Since
\det{V}=-v^{2}
, the transformations that preserve
v^{2}
, or equivalently
\eta_{ab}
, are precisely those with
\det{\Lambda}=1
, that is,
\Lambda\in{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb{C})
.
However,
\Lambda=-\mathds{1}
is not effective on
V
, whence
{\mathrm{SL}}(2,\mathbb{C})
is a double cover of
{\mathrm{SO}}(3,1)
.
128
128

128

Note, however, that
\Lambda=-\mathds{1}
is effective in
\psi^{\prime}=\Lambda\psi
, in perfect agreement with
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,1)
being the double cover of
{\mathrm{SO}}(3,1)
.

The above also explains the index structure
\smash[b]{\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}}
, which is needed for
equation

B.19
to make sense in index-notation,
V^{\prime}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}=\mathchoice{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\gamma}}}_{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.53687pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.81206pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\gamma}}}_{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.53687pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.81206pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\gamma}}}_{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.53687pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.81206pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\gamma}}}_{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.20052pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.53687pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.81206pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{\bar{\Lambda}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\dot{\delta}}}}_{{{\dot{\beta}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{\Lambda}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\dot{\delta}}}}_{{{\dot{\beta}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{\Lambda}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\dot{\delta}}}}_{{{\dot{\beta}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\bar{\Lambda}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\dot{\delta}}}}_{{{\dot{\beta}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}V_{\gamma\dot{\delta}}
.
This being a Lorentz transformation, that is,
V^{\prime}=v^{\prime}_{a}\sigma^{a}
where
v^{\prime}_{a}=\mathchoice{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{\Lambda^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}v_{b}
, further implies that
\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}
is an invariant tensor under
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,1)
.

As already explained,

\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
-1&0\end{pmatrix}^{{{{\mkern-6.0mu}\alpha\beta}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.39986pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.39986pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.57278pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.88533pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}},\qquad\quad\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.39986pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.39986pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.57278pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.88533pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{{\mkern-6.0mu}\alpha\beta}}},

(B.20)

are invariant tensors due to
\det\Lambda=1
in the spinor representation.
Therefore, we can use them to raise and lower spinor indices.
129
129

129

Dotted indices are raised and lowered using the complex conjugates
\bar{\epsilon}^{\dot{\alpha}\dot{\beta}}
and
\bar{\epsilon}_{\dot{\alpha}\dot{\beta}}
, which, in our basis, coincide numerically with
\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}
and
\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}
.

We do this by left-multiplication, that is, it is always the rightmost index of
\epsilon
which is contracted with the quantity whose index is being raised or lowered (
\psi^{\alpha}=\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\psi_{\beta}
).
Note that
\epsilon^{\alpha\gamma}\epsilon^{\beta\delta}\epsilon_{\gamma\delta}=\epsilon^{\beta\alpha}\neq\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}
, whence we cannot raise or lower indices on the
\epsilon
-tensors themselves.
This peculiarity is not a problem since two contracted
\epsilon
-tensors can always be written with a Kronecker delta.
Furthermore, these conventions imply that

\psi_{\alpha}\chi^{\alpha}=\psi_{\alpha}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\chi_{\beta}=-\psi^{\beta}\chi_{\beta}.

(B.21)

Because of this, we need a convention for how to place the indices when switching between index notation and index-free notation.
We use the convention that undotted indices are contracted up-down, while dotted indices are contracted down-up, that is,

\psi\chi=\psi^{\alpha}\chi_{\alpha}=\chi^{\alpha}\psi_{\alpha}=\chi\psi,\qquad\quad\bar{\psi}\bar{\chi}=\bar{\psi}_{\dot{\alpha}}\bar{\chi}^{\dot{\alpha}}=\bar{\chi}_{\dot{\alpha}}\bar{\psi}^{\dot{\alpha}}=\bar{\chi}\bar{\psi},

(B.22)

for anticommuting (Grassmann-odd) spinors.
Due to how complex conjugation is defined on Grassmann numbers, see
appendix

F
, this implies that
(\psi\chi)^{\ast}=\bar{\psi}\bar{\chi}
.

The complex conjugated Pauli matrices
\bar{\sigma}^{a\dot{\alpha}\beta}
are obtained from
\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}
by complex conjugation and raising the indices.
Numerically, in our basis and with the above index structure, they are
\bar{\sigma}^{a}=(-\mathds{1},-\sigma^{i})^{a}
.
In index notation, the statement that
\sigma^{a}
are Hermitian reads
\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}=\bar{\sigma}^{a}_{\dot{\beta}\alpha}
.

One can show that

\sigma^{(a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}\bar{\sigma}^{b)\dot{\beta}\gamma}=-\eta^{ab}\delta_{\alpha}^{\gamma},\qquad\quad\bar{\sigma}^{(a|\dot{\alpha}\beta}\sigma^{|b)}_{\beta\dot{\gamma}}=-\eta^{ab}\delta^{\dot{\alpha}}_{\dot{\beta}},

(B.23)

where the latter is obtained by complex conjugation of the former.
This is equivalent to the Dirac algebra
\{\gamma^{a},\gamma^{b}\}=2\eta^{ab}
, with
\gamma^{a}
from
equation

B.17
.
Using
equation

B.23
, we find
\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}\bar{\sigma}^{b\dot{\beta}\alpha}=-2\eta^{ab}
since the left-hand side is symmetric in
a\,b
due to
\sigma^{a}
being Hermitian.
We can also derive a type of Fierz identity by writing
\smash[b]{V_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}=v_{a}\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}}
.
Contracting with
\bar{\sigma}^{b\dot{\beta}\alpha}
, we find
-2v^{b}=\smash[t]{V_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}\bar{\sigma}^{b\dot{\beta}\alpha}}
and hence

\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\dot{\beta}}\bar{\sigma}_{a}^{\dot{\delta}\gamma}=-2\delta^{\gamma}_{\alpha}\delta^{\dot{\delta}}_{\dot{\beta}}.

(B.24)

Now define
(\sigma^{ab})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}_{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=\sigma^{[a}_{\alpha\dot{\gamma}}\bar{\sigma}^{b]\dot{\gamma}\beta}
.
Using
equation

B.23
, it is straightforward to show that
[\sigma^{ab},\sigma_{cd}]=8\delta^{[a}_{[c}\mathchoice{\sigma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\sigma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\sigma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\sigma^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}
, whence
-\sigma^{ab}/4
are the Lorentz generators in the left-handed spinor representation.
Due to the subtleties when raising and lowering spinor indices,
(\bar{\sigma}^{ab})^{{{\dot{\alpha}}\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77779pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\dot{\beta}}}}=-\bar{\sigma}^{[a|\dot{\alpha}\gamma}\sigma^{|b]}_{\gamma\dot{\beta}}
and
[\bar{\sigma}^{ab},\bar{\sigma}_{cd}]=8\delta^{[a}_{[c}\mathchoice{\bar{\sigma}^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\bar{\sigma}^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\bar{\sigma}^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}{\bar{\sigma}^{{{b]}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.42677pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.9115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.79391pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.78056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.46402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.47429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{d]}}}}
.
Hence,
\bar{\sigma}^{ab}/4
are the Lorentz generators in the right-handed spinor representation, which is consistent with
table

A.1
since
(\sigma^{ab})_{\alpha\beta}
and
(\bar{\sigma}^{ab})_{\dot{\alpha}\dot{\beta}}
are symmetric in
\alpha\,\beta
(
\dot{\alpha}\,\dot{\beta}
).
130
130

130

Note that, due to how we raise and lower indices,
-(L^{ab})^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}
, rather than
(L^{ab})^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}
, are the generators of the dual of the left-handed spinor representation.

This is precisely what is needed for
\gamma^{ab}/4
to be the Lorentz generators in the Dirac spinor representation.

We may define the invariant

\gamma^{5}=-\frac{\mathrm{i}}{4!}\epsilon_{abcd}\gamma^{abcd},

(B.25)

with the properties
(\gamma^{5})^{2}=\mathds{1}
and
\{\gamma^{5},\gamma^{a}\}=0
.
131
131

131

In the context of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(3,1)
, the superscript
5
is not an index.

In the Weyl basis,

(\gamma^{5})^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.01392pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.675pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.625pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}=\begin{pmatrix}\delta_{\alpha}^{\beta}&0\\
0&-\delta^{\dot{\alpha}}_{\dot{\beta}}\end{pmatrix}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.6806pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.6806pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.34169pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.29169pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{B}}}_{{{{\mkern-6.0mu}A}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.383pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.96252pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.83037pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}.

(B.26)

Hence,
\gamma^{5}
may be used to form projection operators
P_{\pm}=(\mathds{1}\pm\gamma^{5})/2
onto the two chiralities.

A real basis

In eleven-dimensional supergravity, we will use Majorana spinors.
Thus, for the compactification to four dimensions, it is convenient with a Majorana basis, in which the
\gamma
-matrices are real.
Such a basis can easily be constructed for instance by letting

\gamma^{0}=\mathrm{i}\sigma^{2}\otimes\sigma^{1},\qquad\gamma^{1}=\sigma^{1}\otimes\sigma^{1},\qquad\gamma^{2}=\sigma^{3}\otimes\sigma^{1},\qquad\gamma^{3}=\mathds{1}\otimes\sigma^{3},

(B.27)

where the Pauli matrices are numerically the same as in
equation

B.18
.
These satisfy the Dirac algebra since the Pauli matrices anticommute and square to
\mathds{1}
.
From
equation

B.25
, it is clear that the chirality projectors
P_{\pm}=(\mathds{1}\pm\gamma^{5})/2
are not real in any basis in which
\gamma^{a}
are real.
Hence, there are no Majorana–Weyl spinors in four dimensions with Lorentzian signature.

B.4
Spinors in eleven dimensions

A spinor in eleven dimensions has 32 components.
In a basis in which the eleven-dimensional
\eta_{\hat{A}\hat{B}}
splits block-diagonally to a four-dimensional
\eta_{ab}
and a seven-dimensional
\delta_{AB}
, we may construct eleven-dimensional
\Gamma
-matrices
\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}}
as

\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}}=(\gamma^{a}\otimes\mathds{1},\ -\gamma^{5}\otimes\Gamma^{A})^{\hat{A}},

(B.28)

where
\gamma^{a}
are the four-dimensional
\gamma
-matrices and
\Gamma^{A}
are the seven-dimensional
\Gamma
-matrices.
132
132

132

That
\gamma^{5}
enters in
\hat{\Gamma}^{A}
corresponds to the fact that the Clifford algebra of the eleven-dimensional space is the
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-
graded
tensor product of the four and seven-dimensional Clifford algebras
[
73
]
.

If we use the Majorana basis from
section

B.3
for
\gamma^{a}
and the basis for
\Gamma^{A}
given in
section

C.1
, we get a basis for
\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}}
in which they are real, that is, a Majorana basis.
133
133

133

Note that
\gamma^{a}
are real while
\Gamma^{a}
and
\gamma^{5}
are imaginary in these bases.

Note that

\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}_{1}\ldots\hat{A}_{11}}=-\epsilon^{\hat{A}_{1}\ldots\hat{A}_{11}}\mathds{1}.

(B.29)

This specifies which of the two inequivalent representations of the Clifford algebra
\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}}
generate.

Since there is precisely one irreducible Dirac spinor representation in eleven dimensions, there must be precisely one irreducible invertible tensor (up to a constant factor)
C^{\alpha\beta}
, where
\alpha
and
\beta
are spinor indices, by Shur’s lemma.
Suppose that there exists
C_{\pm}
such that
C_{\pm}\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}}=\pm(\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}})^{\mathrm{T}}C_{\pm}
.
Since
\pm(\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}})^{\mathrm{T}}
satisfy the Clifford algebra,
C_{\pm}
are intertwiners between different representations of the Clifford algebra.
However, with
\hat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{T}\,\hat{A}_{1}\ldots\hat{A}_{n}}\coloneqq(\hat{\Gamma}^{[\hat{A}_{1}})^{\mathrm{T}}\ldots(\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}_{n}]})^{\mathrm{T}}
,

\hat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{T}\,\hat{A}_{1}\ldots\hat{A}_{11}}=(\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}_{11}\ldots\hat{A}_{1}})^{\mathrm{T}}=+\epsilon^{\hat{A}_{1}\ldots\hat{A}_{11}}\mathds{1},

(B.30)

whence
\hat{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{T}\,\hat{A}}
generate the other, inequivalent, irreducible representation of the Clifford algebra.
Thus,
C_{+}
cannot exist.
134
134

134

Assuming that
C_{+}
exists, we find

which contradicts

By a similar argument,

\hat{\Gamma}^{\hat{A}}
and

In the following, we write

since

and
1
acting as a multiplicative identity both from the left and right.
Here, the structure constants

136

We use
\delta_{ab}
and its inverse to raise and lower indices.

a_{abc}=1,\quad\text{for}\ abc=123,257,536,374,761,642,415,

(C.2)

and the multiplication is extended to all of
\mathbb{O}
as to be distributive over addition.
Using the index split
a=(\hat{\imath},0,i)
, this may be written as

a_{\hat{\imath}\hat{\jmath}\hat{k}}=\epsilon_{ijk},\qquad a_{ij\hat{k}}=-\epsilon_{ijk},\qquad a_{0i\hat{\jmath}}=-\delta_{ij}.

(C.3)

As presented, the construction might seem arbitrary but the octonions fit into the sequence
\mathbb{R}
,
\mathbb{C}
,
\mathbb{H}
,
\mathbb{O}
,
\mathbb{S}
,
\ldots
where
\mathbb{H}
are the quaternions,
\mathbb{S}
the sedenions and every entry is obtained from the previous one through the Cayley–Dickson construction
[
111
]
.
In each step in this sequence, some structure is lost.
For instance, the complex numbers cannot be ordered in a way compatible with multiplication and the quaternions do not commute.
137
137

137

Another, purely algebraic, structure that is lost is that not every complex number is real in the sense that
x^{*}=x
is not generally true for
x\in\mathbb{C}
.

In the step to the octonions, associativity is lost.
This means that the associator

[x,y,z]=(xy)z-x(yz)

(C.4)

is, in general, nonzero for
x,y,z\in\mathbb{O}
.
However, the associator is completely antisymmetric, whence

x(xy)=(xx)y,\qquad(xy)y=x(yy),

(C.5)

for arbitrary
x,y\in\mathbb{O}
.
Thus, the octonions are said to be alternative.
This property is lost in the next step; the sedenions are nonalternative.
138
138

138

The sedenions do, however, satisfy the weaker property of power-associativity,
x(xx)=(xx)x
.

Octonion conjugation is defined as

1^{\ast}=1,\qquad o_{a}^{\ast}=-o_{a}.

(C.6)

This lets us define a scalar product as

\langle x,y\rangle=\operatorname{Re}(x^{\ast}y),

(C.7)

which coincides with the standard scalar product on
\mathbb{R}^{8}
in the basis we have taken and induces a norm

\|x\|^{2}=\langle x,x\rangle=x^{\ast}x=xx^{\ast},

(C.8)

which is then the standard norm on
\mathbb{R}^{8}
.
This norm satisfies

\|xy\|=\|x\|\|y\|,

(C.9)

whence the octonions are said to be a normed division algebra
[
111
]
.
This implies that there are no zero-divisors; if
x
and
y
are nonzero,
xy
is also nonzero.
That there are no zero-divisors can also be seen by noting that, due to alternativity,

x^{\ast}(xy)=(x^{\ast}x)y=\|x\|^{2}y,

(C.10)

whence multiplication by a nonzero
x
is inverted by multiplying by

x^{-1}=\frac{x^{\ast}}{\|x\|^{2}}.

(C.11)

Similarly, the proof of
equation

C.9
is

\|xy\|^{2}=(xy)(y^{\ast}x^{\ast})=x(yy^{\ast})x^{\ast}=\|x\|^{2}\|y\|^{2}.

(C.12)

Here, we have used
(xy)^{\ast}=y^{\ast}x^{\ast}
and the fact that
x
,
y
,
x^{\ast}
and
y^{\ast}
all belong to the associative subalgebra generated by
\operatorname{Im}x
and
\operatorname{Im}y

[
111
]
.

An automorphism of the octonion algebra is, per definition, an
\mathbb{R}
-linear invertible map
g\colon\mathbb{O}\to\mathbb{O}
preserving the octonion multiplication, that is,

\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{O}\qquad g(xy)=g(x)g(y).

(C.13)

The automorphisms naturally form a group,
\operatorname{Aut}\mathbb{O}
, with composition as group multiplication.
This is one way to define the exceptional Lie group
G_{2}
, and the definition we choose in this thesis.
It is worth pointing out that
g(1)=1
for any
g\in G_{2}
, which is immediate from the definition.
Also, automorphisms preserve the scalar product,
\delta_{ab}
and
a_{abc}
.
The Lie algebra
\mathfrak{g}_{2}=\operatorname{Lie}(G_{2})
is the derivation algebra
\mathop{\mathfrak{der}}(\mathbb{O})
of
G_{2}=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{O})
, that is, the linear transformations
D\colon\mathbb{O}\to\mathbb{O}
satisfying

\forall\,x,y\in\mathbb{O}\qquad D(xy)=xD(y)+D(x)y,

(C.14)

and is the compact real form of the exceptional Lie algebra with the same name.

C.1
{\mathrm{Spin}}(7)
, octonions and
G_{2}

Denote the
\mathbb{R}
-linear map from
\mathbb{O}
to itself defined by left-multiplication by
x\in\mathbb{O}
by
L_{x}
.
Two such maps can be composed but since the associator is nonvanishing

L_{x}L_{y}(z)\coloneqq L_{x}(L_{y}(z))=x(yz)\neq(xy)z=L_{xy}(z),

(C.15)

in general.
However, due to alternativity

\displaystyle\{L_{x},L_{y}\}z

\displaystyle=x(yz)+y(xz)=(xy)z-[x,y,z]+(yx)z-[y,x,z]=

\displaystyle=(xy+yx)z=L_{\{x,y\}}z.

(C.16)

Thus, since
\{o_{a},o_{b}\}=-2\delta_{ab}
,

\{L_{o_{a}},L_{o_{b}}\}=-2\delta_{ab}.

(C.17)

This is
almost
identical to the anticommutator of two gamma matrices.
To fix the sign, consider the complexified octonions
\mathbb{C}\otimes\mathbb{O}
and define

\Gamma_{a}\coloneqq-\mathrm{i}L_{o_{a}}.

(C.18)

Since these satisfy the correct anticommutation relations,
\mathbb{C}\otimes\mathbb{O}
can be identified with the Dirac spinor representation of
\operatorname{Spin}(7)
.
To derive the matrix representation of
\Gamma_{a}
consider
\Gamma_{a}o_{A}
where
A=(\hat{0},a)
and
o_{\hat{0}}=1\in\mathbb{O}
.
From the definition,
\Gamma_{a}1=-\mathrm{i}o_{a}

C.2
Structure constant identities

In this section we present some useful relations for the octonion structure constants.
Recall

\displaystyle(\Gamma_{a})_{b{\hat{0}}}=-\mathrm{i}\delta_{ab},\qquad(\Gamma_{a})_{bc}=+\mathrm{i}a_{abc},

Now define the dual of the structure constants

(C.33)

Clearly,

\displaystyle=6\mathchoice{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.05411pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.32434pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[e}}}_{{{[ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.64268pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.6019pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.05411pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.32434pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[e}}}_{{{[ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.64268pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.6019pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.05411pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.32434pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[e}}}_{{{[ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.64268pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.6019pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[10.11821pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.05411pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.32434pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[e}}}_{{{[ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.05801pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.64268pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.6019pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\delta_{c]}^{f]},

(C.46a)

\displaystyle c_{abcd}a^{cde}

\displaystyle=4\mathchoice{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.693pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.35213pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{e}}}_{{{ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.28157pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.62968pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.693pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.35213pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{e}}}_{{{ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.28157pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.62968pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.693pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.35213pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{e}}}_{{{ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.28157pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.62968pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.85431pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.693pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.35213pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{e}}}_{{{ab}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.79411pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.28157pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.62968pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}},

(C.46b)

\displaystyle c_{abcd}a^{bcd}

\displaystyle=0.

(C.46c)

Using the above, it is easy to show that

(C.47)

Lastly, there is a useful identity

\mathchoice{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[11.04129pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[9.17232pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[b_{1}}}}_{{{[a_{1}a_{2}}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.71402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.72429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[11.04129pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[9.17232pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[b_{1}}}}_{{{[a_{1}a_{2}}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.71402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.72429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[11.04129pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[9.17232pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[b_{1}}}}_{{{[a_{1}a_{2}}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.71402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.72429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[16.83919pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[11.04129pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[9.17232pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{[b_{1}}}}_{{{[a_{1}a_{2}}\mathchoice{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[8.73056pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[5.71402pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[4.72429pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[9.55154pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[9.55154pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[6.2012pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[5.07227pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b_{2}b_{3}]}}}_{{{a_{3}]}\mathchoice{\makebox[15.19722pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[15.19722pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[10.06693pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[8.47636pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{a^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[9.55154p
