which can be proven straightforwardly by checking it for all index combinations.

Appendix D
Differential forms

Differential forms are essentially antisymmetric tensors.
Here, we give a brief introduction to some relevant concepts, state our conventions and introduce an index-free formalism.
Consider a connected oriented pseudo-Riemannian
d
-dimensional manifold
\mathcal{M}
without boundary and let
\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})
denote the space of (sufficiently smooth)
p
-forms on
\mathcal{M}
.
On a coordinate chart, we may write
\alpha\in\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})
as

\alpha=\frac{1}{p!}\mathrm{d}x^{m_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{p}}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}(x),

(D.1)

where
\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}
is completely antisymmetric.
142
142

142

Note that we use different conventions for superdifferential forms in superspace, see
section

2.2.3
.

Since the manifold is oriented, there is a canonical volume form

\mathrm{vol}=\frac{\sqrt{|g|}}{d!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}\mathrm{d}x^{m_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d}},

(D.2)

where
\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}
is the covariant Levi-Civita symbol, the covariant tensor density of weight
+1
with
\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{1\ldots d}=+1
, and
g
is the determinant of the metric of tensor-density-weight
-2
.
Equivalently, this may be written as

\sqrt{|g|}\,\mathrm{d}x^{m_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d}}=\bar{\varepsilon}^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}\mathrm{vol},

(D.3)

where
\bar{\varepsilon}^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}
is the contravariant Levi-Civita symbol, that is, the contravariant tensor density of weight
-1
with
\bar{\varepsilon}^{1\ldots d}=+1
.
Note that, since
\sqrt{|g|}
is a pseudo-tensor density of weight
-1
, the volume form is a pseudo-tensor density of weight
0
.
Also, we use different symbols
\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}
and
\bar{\varepsilon}
to distinguish between the covariant and contravariant permutation symbols since

g_{m_{1}n_{1}}\ldots g_{m_{d}n_{d}}\bar{\varepsilon}^{n_{1}\ldots n_{d}}=\bar{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}=g\,\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}.

(D.4)

Using the metric, we may define a pointwise inner product of
p
-forms
\alpha
and
\beta
as
143
143

143

For this to be positive definite, we need to restrict to Euclidean signature.

(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{1}{p!}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}\beta_{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}}g^{m_{1}n_{1}}\ldots g^{m_{p}n_{p}}.

(D.5)

The normalisation here is chosen such that, in the flat Euclidean case,
g_{mn}=\delta_{mn}
, the pointwise norm
\|\alpha\|^{2}=(\alpha,\alpha)
is
1
for
\alpha=\mathrm{d}x^{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{p}
where
p\leq d
.
To see this, note that the tensor representation of
\mathrm{d}x^{1}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{p}
has a
\pm 1
on every position which is a permutation of
1,\ldots,p
, whence the contraction with the metric in
equation

D.5
gives
p!
which is then cancelled by the prefactor
1/p!
.

D.1
The Hodge dual

Using the volume form and the pointwise inner product, we can define the Hodge star operator
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\colon\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\to\Omega^{d-p}(\mathcal{M})
by

\forall\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\colon\qquad\alpha\wedge(\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\beta)=(\alpha,\beta)\mathrm{vol}.

(D.6)

Here,
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\beta
is referred to as the Hodge dual of
\beta
.
The Hodge star operator is linear and well defined
[
112
]
.
Note that
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}1=\mathrm{vol}
since, by the definition,

\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}1=1\wedge\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}1=(1,1)\,\mathrm{vol}=\mathrm{vol},

(D.7)

where
1
is interpreted as the constant function on
\mathcal{M}
with value
1
.
Explicitly,

\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\alpha=\frac{\sqrt{|g|}}{p!(d-p)!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}g^{m_{1}n_{1}}\ldots g^{m_{p}n_{p}}\alpha_{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}}\mathrm{d}x^{m_{p+1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d}}.

(D.8)

This is seen from

\displaystyle\alpha\wedge\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\beta

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p!}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}\mathrm{d}x^{m_{1}}\wedge\ldots\mathrm{d}x^{m_{p}}\wedge

\displaystyle\quad\wedge\frac{\sqrt{|g|}}{p!(d-p)!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{n_{1}\ldots n_{d}}g^{n_{1}q_{1}}\ldots g^{n_{p}q_{p}}\beta_{q_{1}\ldots q_{p}}\mathrm{d}x^{n_{p+1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{n_{d}}=

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p!^{2}(d-p)!}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}\beta^{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{n_{1}\ldots n_{d}}\bar{\varepsilon}^{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}n_{p+1}\ldots n_{d}}\mathrm{vol}=

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p!}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}\beta^{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}\mathrm{vol}=(\alpha,\beta)\mathrm{vol},

(D.9)

where, in the second to last step, we have used

\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{n_{1}\ldots n_{d}}\bar{\varepsilon}^{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}n_{p+1}\ldots n_{d}}=p!(d-p)!\,\delta_{n_{1}}^{m_{1}}{}_{\ldots}^{\ldots}{}_{n_{p}}^{m_{p}}.

(D.10)

Since
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\alpha
is a
(d-p)
-form, its components are read off as

(\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\alpha)_{m_{p+1}\ldots m_{d}}=\frac{\sqrt{|g|}}{p!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}\alpha^{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}.

(D.11)

From this, it follows that

\displaystyle\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}^{2}\alpha

\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{|g|}}{p!(d-p)!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}(\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\alpha)^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d-p}}\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d-p+1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d}}=

\displaystyle=\frac{|g|}{p!^{2}(d-p)!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}^{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}m_{1}\ldots m_{d-p}}\alpha_{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}}\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d-p+1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d}}=

\displaystyle=(-1)^{p(d-p)}\frac{\operatorname{sign}{g}}{p!^{2}(d-p)!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{d-p+1}\ldots m_{d}m_{1}\ldots m_{d-p}}\bar{\varepsilon}^{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}m_{1}\ldots m_{d-p}}\alpha_{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}}\cdot

\displaystyle\quad\cdot\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d-p+1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{d}}=

\displaystyle=(-1)^{p(d-p)}\operatorname{sign}{g}\,\frac{1}{p!}\alpha_{n_{1}\ldots n_{p}}\mathrm{d}x^{n_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{n_{p}}=(-1)^{p(d-p)}\operatorname{sign}{g}\>\alpha,

\displaystyle\therefore\quad\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}^{2}

\displaystyle=(-1)^{p(d-p)}\operatorname{sign}{g}.

(D.12)

Thus, the Hodge star operator gives a natural isomorphism
\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\simeq\Omega^{d-p}(\mathcal{M})
.
Note that
\operatorname{sign}g
only depends on the signature of the metric and is
+1
(
-1
) for Euclidean (Lorentzian) signature.

D.2
The exterior derivative and de Rham cohomology

Differential forms can be differentiated in a coordinate-independent manner without the use of a covariant derivative.
The exterior derivative,
\mathrm{d}
, is the unique linear operator
\mathrm{d}\colon\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\to\Omega^{p+1}(\mathcal{M})
satisfying

\displaystyle f\in\Omega^{0}(U),\quad

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}f=\mathrm{d}x^{m}\partial_{m}f,

(D.13a)

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}^{2}=0,

(D.13b)

\displaystyle\alpha\in\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M}),\quad

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}(\alpha\wedge\beta)=\mathrm{d}\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{p}\alpha\wedge\mathrm{d}\beta,

(D.13c)

where
U\subseteq\mathcal{M}
is any coordinate patch
[
112
]
.
In local coordinates, for a
p
-form
\alpha
,

\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\alpha=\frac{1}{p!}\partial_{n}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}\mathrm{d}x^{n}\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{p}},

(D.14a)

\displaystyle(\mathrm{d}\alpha)_{nm_{1}\ldots m_{p}}=(p+1)\partial_{[n}\alpha_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}]}.

(D.14b)

Note that we may replace the partial derivative,
\partial_{n}
, by the Levi-Civita connection, that is, the unique metric-compatible torsion-free affine connection,
\nabla_{n}
.
This follows from the Christoffel symbols being symmetric in their lower indices.

A
p
-form
\alpha
is said to be closed if
\mathrm{d}\alpha=0
and exact if
\alpha=\mathrm{d}\beta
for some
(p-1)
-form
\beta
.
Note that all exact
p
-forms are closed since
\mathrm{d}^{2}=0
.
Hence, the image of
\mathrm{d}\colon\Omega^{p-1}(\mathcal{M})\to\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})
is a linear subspace of the kernel of
\mathrm{d}\colon\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\to\Omega^{p+1}(\mathcal{M})
and we may define

H^{p}(\mathcal{M})\coloneqq\frac{\ker\bigl(\mathrm{d}\colon\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\to\Omega^{p+1}(\mathcal{M})\bigr)}{\operatorname{im}\bigl(\mathrm{d}\colon\Omega^{p-1}(\mathcal{M})\to\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})\bigr)}.

(D.15)

H^{p}(\mathcal{M})
is a (quotient) vector space known as the
p
’th de Rham cohomology group of
\mathcal{M}

[
112
]
.
Each element of
H^{p}(\mathcal{M})
is an equivalence class, known as a cohomology class,
[\alpha]=\set{\alpha+\mathrm{d}\beta\colon\beta\in\Omega^{p-1}(\mathcal{M})}
where
\mathrm{d}\alpha=0
, that is, it is a closed
p
-form modulo exact
p
-forms.
Based on intuition from
\mathbb{R}^{n}
, one may think that all closed
p
-forms, for
p>0
, are exact, which would render
H^{p}(\mathcal{M})
trivial.
Indeed, this is true for sufficiently nice open subsets of
\mathbb{R}^{n}
(star-shaped) by Poincaré’s lemma
[
112
]
.
However, it is not true in general, the most obvious counterexample being
\mathrm{d}\theta
on a circle, where
\theta
is the usual angular coordinate.
144
144

144

Note that
\theta
is not a global coordinate on
S^{1}
. Clearly,
\mathrm{d}\theta
is exact on the coordinate chart. However, when writing
\mathrm{d}\theta
, we refer to the unique smooth global extension of this local form.

Due to properties of the exterior derivative and since we do not need a metric on
\mathcal{M}
to define the cohomology groups,
b_{p}=\dim H^{p}(\mathcal{M})
are topological invariants of the manifold
[
112
]
.
For compact manifolds,
b_{p}<\infty
is known as the
p
’th Betti number.
Since there are no
-1
-forms and the only closed
0
-forms are locally constant,
\dim H^{0}(\mathcal{M})
is the number of connected components of
\mathcal{M}
(1 for connected
\mathcal{M}
).

Another useful result, which we will use below, is the (generalised) Stokes’ theorem

\int\limits_{\mathcal{M}}\mathrm{d}\alpha=\int\limits_{\partial\mathcal{M}}\alpha,

(D.16)

where
\partial\mathcal{M}
is the boundary of
\mathcal{M}
and
\alpha
is a
(d-1)
-form.
145
145

145

Note that any top form
\alpha
, that is, a
d
-form, can be written as
\alpha(x)=f(x)\mathrm{vol}
.

In particular, if
\mathcal{M}
has no boundary, the integral of an exact form vanishes.
This explains why
\mathrm{d}\theta
on the circle cannot be exact.

D.3
The codifferential

Define the codifferential on
p
-forms by
[
81
]

\delta\coloneqq(-1)^{p}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}^{-1}\mathrm{d}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}=\operatorname{sign}g\,(-1)^{d(p+1)+1}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}.

(D.17)

Note that, while
\mathrm{d}
raises the form-degree by one unit,
\delta
lowers it by one unit.
Clearly,
\delta^{2}=0
by the analogous property of
\mathrm{d}
.
Using the (indefinite) pointwise inner product on
\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})
, we may define
146
146

146

When we do not write out the integration domain, it should be understood that the integral is over all of
\mathcal{M}
.

\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=\int\mathrm{vol}\,(\alpha,\beta).

(D.18)

The codifferential is the formal adjoint of
\mathrm{d}
since, by Stokes’ theorem and the definition of
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}
,

\displaystyle 0

\displaystyle=\int\mathrm{d}(\alpha\wedge\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\beta)=\int\mathrm{d}\alpha\wedge\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\beta-(-1)^{p}\int\alpha\wedge\mathrm{d}(\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\beta)=

\displaystyle=\langle\mathrm{d}\alpha,\beta\rangle-\langle\alpha,\delta\beta\rangle.

(D.19)

where
\alpha
is a
(p-1)
-form and
\beta
a
p
-form.
If
\delta\alpha=0
,
\alpha
is said to be coclosed and, if
\alpha=\delta\beta
, it is said to be coexact.

To find an index-expression for
\delta\alpha
, we first define the pseudo-tensor

\epsilon^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}}\bar{\varepsilon}^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}.

(D.20)

It easy to see that
\epsilon^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}
is covariantly constant with respect to any metric-compatible connection since
\epsilon_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}\epsilon^{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}
is a constant.
From
equations

D.14
and
D.11
, we see that

\displaystyle(\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}\alpha)_{m_{p+2}\ldots m_{d}}

\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{|g|}}{(p+1)!}\underaccent{\bar}{\varepsilon}_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}(p+1)\nabla^{[m_{1}}\alpha^{\ldots m_{p+1}]}=

\displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{sign}g}{p!}\epsilon_{m_{1}\ldots m_{d}}\nabla^{[m_{1}}\alpha^{\ldots m_{p+1}]}.

(D.21)

By using this to compute
\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\mathrm{d}\mathop{}\!\mathord{\star}\alpha
, keeping track of all signs, one finds

(\delta\alpha)_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p-1}}=-\nabla^{n}\alpha_{nm_{1}\dots m_{p-1}}.

(D.22)

D.4
The Hodge–de Rham operator and harmonic forms

Here, we restrict to the case of compact manifolds with Euclidean signature, so that
equation

D.18
is the positive definite inner product of the Hilbert space of
L^{2}
-integrable
p
-forms
[
81
]
.
Using the differential,
\mathrm{d}
, and the codifferential,
\delta
, we can define the Hodge–de Rham operator, or Hodge Laplacian,

\Delta_{p}\coloneqq\delta\mathrm{d}+\mathrm{d}\delta,

(D.23)

which is a second-order differential operator from
\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})
to itself.
Note that
\Delta_{p}
is self-adjoint.
Also,
\Delta_{p}
is nonnegative in the sense that
\langle\alpha,\Delta_{p}\alpha\rangle\geq 0
since
\langle\alpha,\delta\mathrm{d}\alpha\rangle=\langle\mathrm{d}\alpha,\mathrm{d}\alpha\rangle\geq 0
and, similarly,
\langle\alpha,\mathrm{d}\delta\alpha\rangle=\langle\delta\alpha,\delta\alpha\rangle\geq 0
.

If a
p
-form
\alpha
satisfies
\Delta_{p}\alpha=0
, we say that it is harmonic.
147
147

147

This should not be confused with the harmonics of
section

4.2
.

Clearly, a closed, coclosed
p
-form
\alpha
is harmonic.
The converse is also true since, if
\Delta_{p}\alpha=0
,

0=\langle\alpha,\Delta_{p}\alpha\rangle=\langle\alpha,\delta\mathrm{d}\alpha\rangle+\langle\alpha,\mathrm{d}\delta\alpha\rangle=\langle\mathrm{d}\alpha,\mathrm{d}\alpha\rangle+\langle\delta\alpha,\delta\alpha\rangle,

(D.24)

which implies
\mathrm{d}\alpha=0=\delta\alpha
, since the
L^{2}
inner product is positive definite
[
81
]
.

There is an orthogonal decomposition
\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})=\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}\oplus\operatorname{im}\delta_{p+1}
, where the subscripts denote the form-degrees of the differential forms
\mathrm{d}
and
\delta
are acting on.
This is seen by noting that
\alpha\in\ker\mathrm{d}
, that is,
\mathrm{d}_{p}\alpha=0
, is equivalent to
0=\langle\beta,\mathrm{d}_{p}\alpha\rangle=\langle\delta_{p+1}\beta,\alpha\rangle
for all
\beta
, which per definition means that
\alpha\in(\operatorname{im}\delta_{p+1})^{\perp}
.
Hence,
\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}=(\operatorname{im}\delta_{p+1})^{\perp}
, the orthogonal complement of
\operatorname{im}\delta_{p+1}
.
By a completely analogous argument,
\ker\delta_{p}=(\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1})^{\perp}
.
Since all exact forms are closed,
\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1}
is a linear subspace of
\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}
.
Thus, we can make the decomposition
\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}=\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1}\oplus\mathcal{H}^{p}
, where
\mathcal{H}^{p}
is the orthogonal complement of
\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1}
in
\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}
, that is,
\mathcal{H}^{p}=\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}\cap(\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1})^{\perp}
.
148
148

148

Similarly,
\ker\delta_{p}=\operatorname{im}\delta_{p+1}\oplus\mathcal{H}^{p}
.

Putting this together, we have found the orthogonal decomposition

\Omega^{p}(\mathcal{M})=\mathcal{H}^{p}\oplus\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1}\oplus\operatorname{im}\delta_{p+1},\qquad\mathcal{H}^{p}=\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}\cap\ker\delta_{p},

(D.25)

known as the Hodge decomposition
[
81
]
.
Since
\mathcal{H}^{p}
contains all closed, coclosed
p
-forms, it is the space of harmonic
p
-forms.
Also,
\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}=\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1}\oplus\mathcal{H}^{p}
implies that every cohomology class
[\alpha]
contains precisely one harmonic form and

H^{p}(\mathcal{M})=\frac{\ker\mathrm{d}_{p}}{\operatorname{im}\mathrm{d}_{p-1}}\simeq\mathcal{H}^{p}.

(D.26)

Hence, the Betti number
b_{p}
is the dimension of the space of harmonic forms or, equivalently, the dimension of the
0
-eigenspace of
\Delta_{p}
.
Since connected manifolds have
b_{0}=1
, the only harmonic functions on
\mathcal{M}
are constants.
This depends crucially on
\mathcal{M}
being compact so that the integrals converge; the space of harmonic functions on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
is infinite-dimensional.

Appendix E
Bundles, gauge theory and gravity

In this appendix, we give a brief introduction to the concept of bundles and Einstein–Cartan gravity, also known as Cartan’s formulation of general relativity.
To set the stage for Einstein–Cartan gravity, we present a brief review of some aspects of gauge theory after the introduction to fibre bundles.
Although we give some mathematical details, we do not attempt at a complete or mathematically rigorous presentation but rather to give some intuition for the concepts.

E.1
Fibre bundles

A fibre bundle over a manifold is a space that locally looks like the product of the manifold and a fibre but may have a different structure globally.
Formally, it consists of a total space
E
, a base space
\mathcal{M}
, a typical fibre
F
and a projection map
\pi\colon E\to\mathcal{M}
such that for each
x\in\mathcal{M}
there is an open neighbourhood
U_{x}
of
x
and a diffeomorphism
149
149

149

In the setting of topological spaces this is instead a homeomorphism.

\varphi\colon\pi^{-1}(U_{x})\to U_{x}\times F
satisfying
\pi_{1}\circ\varphi=\pi
, where
\pi_{1}\colon U_{x}\times F\to U_{x},
is the natural projection onto the first factor,
(y,f)\mapsto y
,
[
112
,
101
]
.
This means that
U_{x}\times F
and the preimage
\pi^{-1}(U_{x})
, that is, the subset of
E
that maps onto
U_{x}
under the projection, are indistinguishable spaces.
Such a diffeomorphism
\psi
is called a local trivialisation and is the bundle analogue of a coordinate chart of a manifold.
We think of the total space
E
as glued-together fibres with one fibre
F_{x}\simeq F
for each
x\in\mathcal{M}
.

A simple example of a fibre bundle is a cylinder,
S^{1}\times[0,1]
.
Here, the (typical) fibre is
[0,1]
and the base space
S^{1}
.
Since this bundle is globally, and not only locally, a product, it is said to be a trivial bundle.
An example of a nontrivial bundle with the same base space,
S^{1}
, and the same fibre,
[0,1]
, is provided by the Möbius loop.
This only looks like a product
S^{1}\times[0,1]
locally.

There are two types of bundles we are especially interested in, namely, vector bundles and principal bundles.
A vector bundle
E
is a fibre bundle whose fibres,
V_{x}=\pi^{-1}(x)
, and typical fibre,
V=F
, are vector spaces.
Further, it is required that there is a trivialising cover, that is, an open cover of
\mathcal{M}
consisting of local trivialisations, such that the maps
v\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(x,v)
are linear maps between the vector spaces
V
and
\pi^{-1}(x)

[
112
]
.
An example of a vector bundle is the tangent bundle
T\mathcal{M}
, consisting of all tangent spaces of the manifold.
Given two local trivialisations
\varphi_{i,j}
on a pair
U_{i,j}
of intersecting open sets in
\mathcal{M}
, we may consider
\varphi_{ij}=\varphi_{i}\circ\varphi_{j}^{-1}
which is a map from
U\times F
to
U\times F
.
By the properties of
\varphi
, we see that
\varphi_{ij}(x,v)=(x,t_{ij}(x)v)
.
Here,
t_{ij}
is known as a transition function
[
101
]
.
For the tangent bundle, the transition functions are
{\mathrm{GL}}(d,\mathbb{R})
-valued, where
d=\dim\mathcal{M}
, and correspond to local changes of bases on the tangent spaces.

A vector field is a special case of what is known as a section of a bundle.
Technically, it is a map
X\colon\mathcal{M}\to T\mathcal{M}
such that
\pi\circ X=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{M}}
.
Whereas an arbitrary function from
\mathcal{M}
to
T\mathcal{M}
can assign a tangent vector in
T_{y}\mathcal{M}
to a point
x\in\mathcal{M}
, the last requirement ensures that
X
assigns a tangent vector in
T_{x}\mathcal{M}
to
x
.
Differential forms are sections of exterior powers of the cotangent bundle.

The other type of bundles we are interested in is principal bundles.
For these, the fibre is a Lie group
F=G
, known as the structure group, which acts transitively, freely and smoothly from the right on the total space
P

[
101
]
.
The group action is required to be compatible with the bundle structure in the sense that the fibres are preserved, that is,
\pi(p\cdot g)=\pi(p)
, and that, for the local trivialisations
\varphi_{i}\colon\pi^{-1}(U_{i})\to U_{i}\times G
, if
\varphi_{i}(p)=(x,g_{1})
then
\varphi_{i}(p\cdot g_{2})=(x,g_{1}g_{2})
or, equivalently,
\varphi_{i}^{-1}(x,g_{1}g_{2})=\varphi_{i}^{-1}(x,g_{1})\cdot g_{2}
.
This means that the fibres
G_{x}=\pi^{-1}(x)
are
G
-torsors, that is, they are diffeomorphic to
G
but lack a preferred choice of identity element.
The transition functions of a principal
G
-bundle are
G
-valued.

A local trivialisation of a principal bundle
\varphi\colon P\to U\times G
determines an embedding
\phi
of
U
in
P
by
\phi(x)=\varphi^{-1}(x,e)
, where
e
is the identity element of
G
.
150
150

150

This is true for any fibre bundle and one may choose any element of the fibre. For principal bundles, there is a canonical choice provided by
e
. What follows does, however, not hold for arbitrary fibre bundles.

This goes the other way too, given an embedding
\phi\colon U\to P
there is a (unique) local trivialisation
\varphi
defined by
\varphi^{-1}(x,g)=\phi(x)\cdot g
.
Hence, a principal bundle is trivial if, and only if, it admits a global smooth section.

An example of a principal
{\mathrm{GL}}(d,\mathbb{R})
-bundle is the frame bundle, consisting of all bases of all tangent spaces of
\mathcal{M}

[
81
]
.
If we have a metric
g
on
\mathcal{M}
, we may consider the bundle of orthonormal frames.
The transition functions are then restricted to
{\mathrm{O}}(d,\mathbb{R})
.
The orthonormal frame bundle is a subbundle of the frame bundle and we say that we have a reduction of the structure group from
{\mathrm{GL}}(d,\mathbb{R})
to
{\mathrm{O}}(d,\mathbb{R})
.
Such a reduction is always possible since all manifolds admit a Riemannian metric.
In general, there may, however, be obstructions to structure group reductions.
For instance, consider the further reduction from
{\mathrm{O}}(d,\mathbb{R})
to
{\mathrm{SO}}(d,\mathbb{R})
of the structure group of
T\mathcal{M}
.
This is only possible if there is a bundle of frames such that for every
x\in\mathcal{M}
, all frames in the fibre over
x
have the same orientation, which is equivalent to the manifold being orientable.
The Möbius loop, now considered as the base manifold, is not orientable.
Another example is provided by considering a reduction of the tangent group to
\set{e}
, the trivial group.
If such a reduction exists, the tangent bundle is trivial and we say that the manifold is parallelisable.

Similar to the above, one can construct a frame bundle associated with any vector bundle, not only the tangent bundle.
It is also possible to go in the opposite direction and construct an associated vector bundle from a principal bundle.
To this end, suppose that we have a principal
G
-bundle with total space
P
.
To construct the associated vector bundle, we additionally need a vector space
V
and a left-representation
\rho\colon G\to{\mathrm{GL}}(V)
.
Define the right-action
(p,v)\cdot g=(p\cdot g,\rho(g^{-1})v)
of
G
on
P\times V
.
This gives an equivalence relation
(p,v)\sim(p,v)\cdot g
and we denote the set of equivalence classes
[p,v]
by
E=P\times_{\rho}V
.

E
can be given a differentiable structure
[
101
]
and is a vector bundle over
\mathcal{M}
with fibre
V

[
81
]
.
The projection
\pi_{E}\colon E\to\mathcal{M}
is given by
\pi_{E}([p,v])=\pi(p)
.
This is well-defined since, choosing another representative,
\pi_{E}([p\cdot g,\rho(g^{-1})v])=\pi(p\cdot g)=\pi(p)
.
To give a vector space structure to the fibres of
E
, note that any two points in the fibre over
x
can uniquely be written as
[p,v_{1}]
and
[p,v_{2}]
, for any
p\in\pi^{-1}(x)
.
This follows immediately from the requirements on the group action of
G
on
P
.
Now define
[p,v_{1}]+c[p,v_{2}]=[p,v_{1}+cv_{2}]
.
That this addition and scalar multiplication are well-defined is easily seen by taking other representatives of
[p,v_{1,2}]
and using that
\rho
is a linear representation.

A local trivialisation
\varphi\colon\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times G
of
P
induces a local trivialisation of
E
,
\varphi_{E}\colon\pi_{E}^{-1}(U)\to U\times V
, by

\varphi_{E}([p,v])=\bigl(\pi_{1}\circ\varphi(p),\ \rho(\pi_{2}\circ\varphi(p))v\bigr),

(E.1)

where
\pi_{1,2}
are the natural projections onto the first and second factors of
U\times G
, respectively.
By the properties of
\varphi
and
\rho
, this is well-defined.
Also, by restricting to a single fibre, which amounts to fixing
p\in\pi^{-1}(x)
by the above remark, we get a linear map
\pi_{2}\circ\varphi_{E}\colon\pi_{E}^{-1}(x)\to V
(the inverse is
v\mapsto\varphi_{E}^{-1}(x,v)
), which shows that the fibres are isomorphic to
V
.
Lastly, the transition functions of
E
are
\rho(t_{ij})
, where
t_{ij}
are the transition functions of
P
, and take values in
\rho(G)\subseteq{\mathrm{GL}}(V)
.

Sections of an associated bundle
E=P\times_{\rho}V
are in one-to-one correspondence with
G
-equivariant functions
P\to V
.
A function
f\colon P\to V
is said to be
G
-equivariant if
f(p\cdot g)=\rho(g^{-1})f(p)
.
To see the correspondence, suppose that we have such a function
f
.
To construct a section of
E
, simply let
x\mapsto[p,f(p)]
for any
p\in P_{x}
.
This is well-defined since any other point in the same fibre
P_{x}
is of the form
p\cdot g
and
[p\cdot g,f(p\cdot g)]=[p,\rho(g)f(p\cdot g)]=[p,f(p)]
by the equivariance of
f
.
Since
\pi_{E}([p,f(p)])=\pi(p)=x
, this is indeed a section.
To go in the other direction, suppose that we have a section
s
of
E
.
Note that
s\circ\pi(p)
, which is an element of
E_{\pi(p)}
, has a unique representative of the form
(p,v)
for some
v\in V
.
Thus, we can define
f(p)=v
.
Now,
[p,v]=[p\cdot g,\rho(g^{-1})v]
whence
f(p\cdot g)=\rho(g^{-1})v
, that is,
f
is equivariant.
These two constructions are clearly inverse.

As explained above, a local trivialisation
\varphi\colon\pi^{-1}(U)\to U\times G
of
P
induces a local trivialisation
\varphi_{E}\colon\pi_{E}^{-1}(U)\to U\times V
.
For
x\in U
we then have
\varphi_{E}\circ s(x)=(x,v(x))
, whence we may, locally, think of the section
s
of
E
as a
V
-valued function
v(x)
on
U
.
Using that
s(x)=[p,f(p)]
for any
p\in P_{x}
and
equation

E.1
, we find
v(x)=\rho(\pi_{2}\circ\varphi(p))f(p)
.
By choosing
p=\varphi^{-1}(x,e)\eqqcolon\phi(x)
, where
\phi
is the canonical embedding of
U
in
P
as above, we get

v(x)=f(\phi(x)).

(E.2)

E.2
Gauge theory

In a gauge theory with structure group
G
, the fundamental geometrical object is a principal
G
-bundle over
\mathcal{M}
.
151
151

151

In physics,
G
is often referred to as the gauge group (for instance the
{\mathrm{U}}(1)\times{\mathrm{SU}}(2)\times{\mathrm{SU}}(3)
of the Standard Model). We reserve the term gauge group for the gauged structure group, that is, the group of gauge transformations.

Fields that are charged under the gauge group correspond to sections of associated vector bundles.
Thus, to be able to, for instance, write down a kinetic Lagrangian, we need a way of differentiating such sections.

The tangent space
T_{p}P
of the principal bundle
P
at a point
p
contains a subspace that is tangent to the fibre of
P
through
p
, called the vertical subspace and denoted
V_{p}
.
A principal connection on
P
is defined by assigning horizontal subspaces
H_{p}
to each
p
such that
V_{p}\oplus H_{p}=T_{p}P
,
H_{p}
depends smoothly on
p
and is equivariant in the sense that
H_{p\cdot g}
agrees with the pushforward of
H_{p}
along
p\mapsto p\cdot g

[
101
]
.
There is a natural way of identifying
V_{p}
with
\mathfrak{g}=\operatorname{Lie}(G)
and one can, by using this, define a
\mathfrak{g}
-valued 1-form on
P
as the projection onto
V_{p}
in the decomposition
T_{p}P=V_{p}\oplus H_{p}

[
101
]
.
Given a local trivialisation over
U\subseteq\mathcal{M}
, this 1-form can be pulled back to a local
\mathfrak{g}
-valued 1-form
A
on
U
.
In what follows, we use this local description since it is more well-suited for the calculations we are concerned with in the main text, even though this somewhat obscures the geometrical nature of the subject.

Using the local connection form
A
, we define a covariant exterior differential,

\mathcal{D}=\mathrm{d}+A,

(E.3)

acting on the tensor product of the bundle of differential
p
-forms and a bundle associated with the principal bundle.
Locally, a section of such a bundle can be written as
V^{i}=\mathrm{d}x^{m_{1}}\wedge\ldots\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{m_{p}}V_{m_{1}\ldots m_{p}}{}^{i}/p!
, where
i
is an index of some representation of
G
.
152
152

152

We always put the form-indices closest to the symbol on components of
p
-forms with additional indices.

The covariant exterior differential acting on
V^{i}
reads

\mathcal{D}V^{i}=\mathrm{d}V^{i}+A^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}\wedge V^{j}.

(E.4)

Note that the special case of a 0-form is a section of an associated bundle.
A change of local trivialisation of the principal bundle induces a change of trivialisation of the associated vector bundles corresponding to
V^{i}\mapsto V^{\prime i}=g^{{{i}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.71356pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.29834pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.64166pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{j}}}V^{j}
, where
g\in G
depends on the spacetime point.
153
153

153

A change of local trivialisation is a passive gauge transformation.

Demanding that the covariant exterior derivative is covariant, that is,
\mathcal{D}V\mapsto\mathcal{D}^{\prime}V^{\prime}=g\mathcal{D}V
, we get, dropping indices,

\mathcal{D}^{\prime}V^{\prime}=\mathrm{d}(gV)+A^{\prime}\wedge gV=g\,\mathrm{d}V+\mathrm{d}g\wedge V+A^{\prime}\wedge gV=g(\mathrm{d}V+A\wedge V)

(E.5)

whence

A^{\prime}=gAg^{-1}+g\,\mathrm{d}g^{-1},

(E.6)

where we have used that
0=\mathrm{d}(gg^{-1})=(\mathrm{d}g)g^{-1}+g\,\mathrm{d}g^{-1}
.
This transformation law can also be derived from the properties of the global connection form on the principal bundle
[
101
]
.

Given a principal connection, we define its field strength, or curvature 2-form, as

F=\mathrm{d}A+A\wedge A.

(E.7)

Define the operator
\mathcal{F}
by
\mathcal{F}V=F\wedge V
.
Then,

\mathcal{D}^{2}V=\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{d}V+A\wedge V)=(\mathrm{d}A\wedge V-A\wedge\mathrm{d}V)+(A\wedge\mathrm{d}V+A\wedge A\wedge V)=F\wedge V,

(E.8)

that is,
\mathcal{D}^{2}=\mathcal{F}
, which is known as the Bianchi identity of the first type.
Since
\mathcal{D}\mapsto\mathcal{D}^{\prime}=g\mathcal{D}g^{-1}
, this implies that
F\mapsto F^{\prime}=gFg^{-1}
under a change of local trivialisation.
Thus,
F
is a tensorial 2-form transforming under the adjoint representation.
This can also be seen by a straightforward calculation,

F^{\prime}=\mathrm{d}(gAg^{-1}+g\,\mathrm{d}g^{-1})+(gAg^{-1}+g\,\mathrm{d}g^{-1})\wedge(gAg^{-1}+g\,\mathrm{d}g^{-1})=gFg^{-1}.

(E.9)

Clearly,
[\mathcal{D},\mathcal{F}]=0
, which for the 2-form
F
is equivalent to
\mathcal{D}F=0
.
This is the Bianchi identity of the second type and can also be shown as

\mathcal{D}F=\mathcal{D}(\mathrm{d}A+A\wedge A)=(\mathrm{d}A\wedge A-A\wedge\mathrm{d}A)+[A\wedge F]=0,

(E.10)

where
[A\wedge F]=A\wedge F-F\wedge A
appears since
F
transforms under the adjoint representation.

E.3
Einstein–Cartan gravity

In Cartan’s formulation of general relativity, one uses the language of principal bundles and gauge theory to formulate Einstein’s theory of gravity.
On a spacetime of dimension
d
, the structure group is
{\mathrm{Spin}}(d-1,1)
.
The principal connection is referred to as the spin connection and is denoted by
\omega
.
The curvature 2-form is denoted by
R
.
Given a metric of signature
(d-1,1)
, the structure group
{\mathrm{GL}}(d)
of
T\mathcal{M}
may always be reduced to
{\mathrm{SO}}(d-1,1)
, provided
\mathcal{M}
is orientable.
Essentially, this amounts to restricting the frame bundle to the subbundle of positively oriented orthonormal frames.
Spinor fields are, however, sections of a vector bundle associated not to
{\mathrm{SO}}(d-1,1)
but
{\mathrm{Spin}}(d-1,1)
.
Thus, we need a lift of the structure group
{\mathrm{SO}}(d-1,1)
to the double cover
{\mathrm{Spin}}(d-1,1)
, that is, a spin structure, to be able to define spinors.
Apart from the obstructions to orientability
[
73
,
80
]
and the existence of a Lorentzian metric
[
80
]
, there can be further obstructions to such a lift.
Specifically, there is such a lift to
{\mathrm{Spin}}(d-1,1)
if and only if the second Stiefel–Whitney class of
\mathcal{M}
vanishes
[
73
]
.

Assuming that we have a spin structure, there is a bundle of spin frames and we can take a local section
e_{a}=e_{a}{}^{m}\partial_{m}
.
There is a dual frame of the cotangent bundle
e^{a}=\mathrm{d}x^{m}e_{m}{}^{a}
such that
e_{a}{}^{m}e_{m}{}^{b}=\delta_{a}^{b}
and
e_{m}{}^{a}e_{a}{}^{n}=\delta_{m}^{n}
.
These are known as vielbeins or, in the case
d=4
, vierbeins.
154
154

154

“Viel” is German for many while “vier” means four.

The Lorentz indices
a,b,c,\ldots
are referred to as flat and coordinate indices
m,n,p,\ldots
as curved.
The vielbeins are used to convert between the two types of indices.
However, the Lorentz covariant derivate
\mathcal{D}
acts only on flat indices.
This means that we distinguish between, for instance,
T\mathcal{M}
and the associated vector bundle of
{\mathrm{Spin}}(d-1,1)
carrying the vector representation and view
e_{a}{}^{m}
as an isomorphism between them.
In Einstein–Cartan gravity, we therefore only use curved indices as form-indices.

Since we have reduced
{\mathrm{GL}}(d)
to
{\mathrm{SO}}(d-1,1)
by restricting to orthonormal frames, the vielbeins are orthonormal and

g_{mn}=\mathchoice{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{a}}}_{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{a}}}_{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{a}}}_{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{a}}}_{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\mathchoice{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{b}}}_{{{n}\mathchoice{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.51666pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.1029pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.50208pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c (E.11)

The word orthonormal is perhaps only appropriate for
\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,+1,\ldots,+1)_{ab}
.
However, any metric tensor with flat indices and the correct signature can be used.

The torsion 2-form of the spin connection is defined by

(E.12)

which implies that
T_{abc}=2e_{[b}{}^{n}\partial_{a]}e_{nc}-2\omega_{[ab]c}
.
Since the spin connection is antisymmetric in its last two indices, which follows from it being a principal
{\mathfrak{so}}(d-1,1)
connection, we get

\omega_{abc}=\mathring{\omega}_{abc}+\kappa_{abc},\qquad\left\{\begin{aligned} &\mathring{\omega}_{abc}=e_{[b}{}^{n}\partial_{a]}e_{nc}-e_{[c}{}^{n}\partial_{a]}e_{nb}-e_{[c}{}^{n}\partial_{b]}e_{na},\\
&\kappa_{abc}=-\frac{1}{2}\bigl(T_{abc}-T_{acb}-T_{bca}\bigr),\end{aligned}\right.

(E.13)

where
\mathring{\omega}
is the unique torsion-free spin connection and
\kappa_{abc}
is referred to as the contorsion tensor.
Note that
T_{abc}=-2\kappa_{[ab]c}
.
As we will see, this formalism reduces to the ordinary formalism of general relativity if the torsion is constrained to
0
so that

.

Next, we define the affine connection

155

155

]
refers to as a generalised affine connection, namely a principal connection on the bundle of affine frames with an

\nabla
by

(E.14)

We can express

(E.16)

We write
\nabla
also for the total covariant derivative,
\nabla_{m}=\partial_{m}+\varGamma_{m}+\omega_{m}
, acting on both flat and curved indices.
Since the covariant derivate obeys Leibniz’s rule and the definition of the affine connection reads, in terms of the total covariant derivative,
\nabla_{m}V^{n}=\mathchoice{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}\nabla_{m}V^{a}
, this definition implies that

\nabla_{m}\mathchoice{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}_{{{a}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}=0,\qquad\quad\nabla_{m}\mathchoice{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{a}}}_{{{n}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.33765pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.59009pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.85005pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}}{e^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textst (E.17)

This is sometimes referred to as the vielbein postulate.
Since
g_{mn}=\eta_{ab}e_{m}{}^{a}e_{n}{}^{b}
, it immediately follows that
\nabla_{m}g_{np}=0
, that is, the affine connection is metric compatible.
Note that the Lorentz covariant derivate
\mathcal{D}
can always be replaced by the total covariant derivate
\nabla
but the opposite direction is only possible if all indices that
\nabla
acts on are
{\mathrm{Spin}}(d-1,1)
-indices, that is, flat.
In particular,
T^{a}=\nabla e^{a}
and, by the vielbein postulate,

T^{m}\coloneqq e_{a}{}^{m}T^{a}=\nabla\mathrm{d}x^{m}=\mathchoice{\varGamma^{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}}{\varGamma^{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}}{\varGamma^{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}}{\varGamma^{{{m}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.94333pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.94115pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.10081pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[7.09612pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[4.30226pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[3.07304pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{n}}}}\wedge\mathrm{d}x^{n}.

(E.18)

Hence, the torsion vanishes precisely when
\varGamma_{[m}{}^{p}{}_{n]}=0
.
This is just the statement that the unique metric-compatible torsion-free affine connection, that is, the Levi-Civita connection, is symmetric in its lower indices.

The curvature 2-form
R_{a}{}^{b}=\mathrm{d}\omega_{a}{}^{b}+\omega_{a}{}^{c}\wedge\omega_{c}{}^{b}
has components given by

(E.19)

Lastly, consider the action

S=\frac{1}{2\kappa}\int\mathrm{d}^{D}x\,eR,

(E.20)

where

This is known as the Palatini action.
Clearly, it reduces to the Einstein–Hilbert action under the constraint of vanishing torsion since, then, all quantities can be expressed in terms of the metric.
However, we may view the vielbein and spin connection as a priori independent, thereby obtaining a first-order formulation of gravity.
To see that this is classically equivalent to the Einstein–Hilbert action, we need to show that the equation of motion for the spin connection forces it to be torsion-free.
To this end, let

We can make a change of variables and view the contorsion and the vielbein as the fundamental quantities.
Thus, we wish to show that

By the definition of the curvature,

(E.21)

where
\mathring{R}
is the curvature 2-form of
\mathring{\omega}
.

158

Since

(E.22)

Since the contorsion is antisymmetric in its last two indices, the middle term can be written as
2\mathring{\nabla}_{m}\kappa_{n}{}^{mn}
, which is a total derivative not contributing to the equation of motion.
Thus, the equation of motion for
\kappa
is given by the variation of the third term in
equation

E.22
.
A straightforward calculation shows that
\kappa_{mab}=0
on-shell.

When matter is added to the Palatini action, there can be extra terms in the equation of motion for the contorsion.
As long as there are no new terms containing derivatives of
\kappa
, we can still solve for the contorsion in terms of the other fields through its equation of motion.
This means that there are no independent propagating degrees of freedom in the contorsion and that we can eliminate it from the theory by substitution in the Lagrangian.
The interaction terms arising in this way would not be present if we instead constrain the torsion to 0.
However, keeping
\kappa
dynamical, we could just add the negative of these terms to the original Lagrangian to eliminate these interactions ad hoc.
This is essentially the method of Lagrange multipliers.

Appendix F
Grassmann numbers

Grassmann numbers are graded-commutative objects crucial to, for instance, the path integral formulation of theories with fermions and superspace formulations of supersymmetric theories and supergravity.
The Grassmann numbers form a graded algebra over the real or complex numbers.
Here, we introduce some conventions related to Grassmann numbers, in particular concerning differentiation and integration with respect to Grassmann variables.

Let
\theta^{\alpha}
,
\alpha=1,\ldots,n
, be Grassmann variables with a multiplication satisfying

\theta^{\alpha}\theta^{\beta}=-\theta^{\beta}\theta^{\alpha},

(F.1)

generating the Grassmann algebra.
The grading of the algebra simply counts the numbers of Grassmann variables appearing multiplicatively in an expression.
Elements that are even in the grading, for instance
1
and
\theta^{\alpha}\theta^{\beta}
, are called Grassmann-even while elements that are odd in the grading, for instance
\theta^{\alpha}
and
\theta^{\alpha}\theta^{\beta}\theta^{\gamma}
, are Grassmann-odd.
For instance in
D=11
supergravity, we use real Grassmann variables but here we focus on the complex case since the real case is easily inferred.
We define complex conjugation such that

(\theta^{\alpha}\theta^{\beta})^{*}=\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}}\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\alpha}}.

(F.2)

We define differentiation with respect to
\theta^{\alpha}
and
\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\alpha}}
by

\displaystyle\partial_{\alpha}\coloneqq\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta^{\alpha}},\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta^{\alpha}}\theta^{\beta}\coloneqq\delta_{\alpha}^{\beta},\qquad\quad

\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta^{\alpha}}\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}}\coloneqq 0,

(F.3)

\displaystyle\bar{\partial}_{\dot{\alpha}}\coloneqq\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\alpha}}},

\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\alpha}}}\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}}\coloneqq\delta_{\dot{\alpha}}^{\dot{\beta}},

\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\alpha}}}\theta^{\beta}\coloneqq 0,

linearity and the graded Leibniz rule.
Thus,

\partial_{\alpha}(\theta^{\beta_{1}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}})=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta^{\alpha}}(\theta^{\beta_{1}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}})=n\delta_{\alpha}^{[\beta_{1}}\theta^{\beta_{2}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}]}.

(F.4)

If we insist on
equation

F.2
being valid for Grassmann operators and functions as well, this is consistent with

(\partial_{\alpha})^{*}=-\bar{\partial}_{\dot{\alpha}}

(F.5)

since then

\displaystyle\bigl(\partial_{\alpha}(\theta^{\beta_{1}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}})\bigr)^{*}

\displaystyle=\bigl(n\delta_{\alpha}^{[\beta_{1}}\theta^{\beta_{2}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}]}\bigr)^{*}=n\delta_{\dot{\alpha}}^{[\dot{\beta}_{1}}\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}_{n}}\ldots\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}_{2}]}

\displaystyle=-(-1)^{n}\bar{\partial}_{\dot{\alpha}}(\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}_{n}}\ldots\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}_{1}})=(-1)^{n+1}n\delta_{\dot{\alpha}}^{[\dot{\beta}_{n}}\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}_{n-1}}\ldots\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}_{1}]},

(F.6)

and an
n
-cycle has parity
(-1)^{n+1}
.

In
d=4
, we can raise and lower the indices using the antisymmetric
\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}
.
Contrary to how we raise and lower indices on other quantities, the indices on
\partial_{\alpha}
and
\bar{\partial}_{\dot{\alpha}}
are raised and lowered from the right.
This ensures that

\partial^{\alpha}\theta_{\beta}=\delta^{\alpha}_{\beta}\qquad\qquad\bar{\partial}^{\dot{\alpha}}\bar{\theta}_{\dot{\beta}}=\delta^{\dot{\alpha}}_{\dot{\beta}}.

(F.7)

We also want to be able to integrate over Grassmann variables.
For this, we use the Berezin integral

\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\,\theta^{\beta}\coloneqq\delta_{\alpha}^{\beta},\qquad\qquad\int\mathrm{d}\bar{\theta}_{\dot{\alpha}}\,\bar{\theta}^{\dot{\beta}}\coloneqq\delta_{\dot{\alpha}}^{\dot{\beta}}.

(F.8)

Note that
\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}
should be interpreted as the integration measure for
\theta^{\alpha}
, even though the index position is different.
Also, the dimension of the measure is opposite to that of the Grassmann variable to make the integral dimensionless.
The integration measure
\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}
should not be confused with the superdifferential form
\mathrm{d}\theta^{\alpha}
; it should always be clear from the context which of the two is being referred to.
If we make a change of variables
\theta^{\alpha}\mapsto\mathchoice{S^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}}{S^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}}{S^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}}{S^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\beta}}}}\theta^{\beta}
we see that the measure has to transform like
\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\mapsto\mathrm{d}\theta_{\beta}\mathchoice{{S^{-1}}^{{{\beta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}}}}{{S^{-1}}^{{{\beta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}}}}{{S^{-1}}^{{{\beta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}}}}{{S^{-1}}^{{{\beta}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}}}}
.
This also motivates

\mathrm{d}\theta^{\alpha}=\mathrm{d}\theta_{\beta}\epsilon^{\beta\alpha},

(F.9)

similar to how the index on
\partial_{\alpha}
was raised.

By requiring graded linearity we get

\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\,\theta^{\beta_{1}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}}=n\delta_{\alpha}^{[\beta_{1}}\theta^{\beta_{2}}\ldots\theta^{\beta_{n}]}.

(F.10)

Note that this means that the integration operator and differential operator can be identified

\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}=\partial_{\alpha}.

(F.11)

These considerations go through completely analogously for dotted indices.
In particular, this means that

\bigl(\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\bigr)^{*}=-\int\mathrm{d}\bar{\theta}_{\dot{\alpha}}.

(F.12)

In
d=4
dimensions we also define

\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\theta\,\theta^{2}\coloneqq 1,\qquad\qquad\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\bar{\theta}\,\bar{\theta}^{2}\coloneqq 1.

(F.13)

This is consistent with

\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{4}\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\beta}

(F.14)

since

\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\beta}\epsilon_{\gamma\delta}\theta^{\gamma}\theta^{\delta}=2\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\epsilon_{\gamma\delta}\int\mathrm{d}\theta_{\alpha}\,\delta_{\beta}^{[\gamma}\theta^{\delta]}=2\epsilon^{\alpha\beta}\epsilon_{\gamma\delta}\delta_{\alpha\beta}^{\delta\gamma}=4.

(F.15)

From the above, it is also clear that

\Bigl(\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\theta\Bigl)^{\ast}=\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\bar{\theta}.

(F.16)

Hence, we can identify

\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{4}\partial^{\alpha}\partial_{\alpha}=\frac{1}{4}\partial^{2},\qquad\quad\int\mathrm{d}^{2}\bar{\theta}=\frac{1}{4}\bar{\partial}_{\dot{\alpha}}\bar{\partial}^{\dot{\alpha}}=\frac{1}{4}\bar{\partial}^{2}.

(F.17)
